001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.name: Garden Mosque
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.holder: Baden-Württemberg Castles and Gardens, State Agency for Property Assets and Construction
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.dates: The mosque complex comprises a cloister-like colonnade in the east (1779–84) and a main building (1782–86) flanked by two minarets (1786–95) in the west
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.author: Hartmut Troll
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.history:
The mosque in the Schwetzingen palace gardens today is the last surviving example of a type of building quite common in European landscape gardens up to the end of the 18th-century.  
The mosque, built 1782–95 by Nicolas de Pigage, was preceded by the Ambulatory, designed inside a Turkish Garden, which was first mentioned in 1774. Work on the actual mosque building started after Elector Carl Theodor had moved to Munich. The Ambulatory itself already represents contemporaneous ideas of what a mosque building looked like; the similarities with the feature of the holy sites of Mecca, published by Fischer von Erlach, are as unmistakable as the similarity of the corner pavilions with the mosque built by Chambers at Kew Gardens. The mosque itself is a fairly autonomous structure with a temple-like portico and Baroque dome.
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.keywords: Garden Building; Turkish garden; Arabic inscriptions; minarets; Mosque; Moorish style; Romanticism; gardens
001f116f-84e2-522a-b67a-25d887e4cb0a.description2: The mosque is surrounded by a “Turkish garden” with winding paths and exotic plants. The architectural feature of the central building provides an original variation on the language of shapes found in baroque churches. Quotations from the western architectural history are combined with oriental motifs and inscriptions from the Qur'an. The minarets are positioned slightly in front of the western façade. The colonnade walkway with its rectangular layout is comprised of latticework open on all sides. The octagonal pavilions are decorated with dictums in Arabic and German. One striking feature is the refined roofscape with different basic slatecovered shapes, adorned by innumerable gilded crescents. The mosque’s interior is comprised of a round central hall, richly and colourfully decorated. Various general maxims are inscribed in Arabic and translated into German. These texts are not religious in nature, but generally invoke virtues, such as wisdom, diligence and discretion.

01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.name: Çırağan Palace
01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.keywords: Photograph; Old İstanbul Photograph; İstanbul; Pascal Sebah
01309821-1550-570d-b610-d7e90337db0f.description2: Pascal Sébah (1823-86) was a pioneer photographer who worked in Istanbul. In 1857 he opened his first photography studio in Istanbul. Çırağan Palace, built by Sultan Abdülâziz, was designed by the palace architect Nigoğayos Balyan and constructed by his sons Sarkis and Hagop Balyan between 1863 and 1867. This was a period in which all Ottoman sultans used to build their own palaces rather than using those of their ancestors. Çırağan Palace is the last example of this period. The inner walls and the roof were made of wood, the outer walls of colourful marble. The palace is connected with a beautiful marble bridge to the Yıldız Palace on the hill behind. A very high garden wall protects the palace from the outer world.

01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.name: *The Aqueduct in the Forest of Belgrade, Istanbul*
01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
01438940-6e4b-5dae-9321-45c0f28c82d7.description2: This painting by an anonymous Ottoman artist shows the aqueduct of Belgrade Forest outside Istanbul. Istanbul’s water was stored in the reservoirs of Belgrade Forest and conveyed to the city across a number of aqueducts like this one. Established in early Ottoman times, the Istanbul water supply system was expanded and improved throughout the Ottoman period, incorporating complex systems of reservoirs, aqueducts and supply pipes endling in fountains and waterspouts.

031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.name: The museum of 'rare possessions'
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.author: Ibrahim Abdel Aziz
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.history: Princess Fatma Ismail (1853–1920) was one of Khedive Ismail's daughters. She married Prince Tusun ibn Muhammad Sa`id Pasha, alderman of Egypt, in 1871. She is distinguished from her sisters by her philanthropic contributions to culture and science. Princess Fatma took the initiative of dismissing the university from its financial crisis by providing it with an endowment. She also donated jewellery to provide the university with much-needed cash and land for the campus to be built on. She participated in laying the foundation stone of the university. She passed away before seeing the university built.
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.keywords: Agricultural museum; Fatma Ismail; Palace; Khedive Ismail; Khedive; agriculture; museum
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.second_name: Fatma Ismail’s Palace Museum at the Agricultural museum; The Antiquity Collection Museum
031df7be-4492-57dc-b989-693ca01a17f1.description2: This building was once the villa of Fatma Ismail, daughter of Khedive Ismail, and now it is a museum that houses over 500 rare pieces of art dating to the late 19th and early 20th centuries. When the palace was built and then restored, Egyptian architecture was being influenced by the European trends of the time (Italian and French). Italian and French architects were designing and building edifices for the Egyptian elite.

055fd98c-bc6c-5a97-9aae-e3c3ab6ea7fb.name: Plan of Bullring of Campo Pequeno, Lisbon
055fd98c-bc6c-5a97-9aae-e3c3ab6ea7fb.keywords: Rediscovering the Past; Cities; Urban Spaces
055fd98c-bc6c-5a97-9aae-e3c3ab6ea7fb.description2: Built in an area assigned to the Casa Pia by the city of Lisbon in 1889 Praça de Touros do Campo Pequeno (Campo Pequeno Bullring) was designed by the architect António José Dias da Silva (1848-1912) and inspired by the Madrid's bullring. Praça de Touros do Campo Pequeno opened its doors on August 18, 1892, with a gala show.

057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.name: Saliha Sultan Fountain
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.description2: Robertson’s photographs of landscapes and monuments were usually printed in a roughly 25 by 30cm format. In the early years of his career as a photographer, he appears to have preferred the albumen-on-glass method of taking negatives, switching to the wet collodion process around 1855. For his positive prints, he used salt paper until about 1858; after that, prints were made on albumen paper even if they were made from negatives taken before that year. Robertson’s photographs are concentrated mainly in and around the districts known as Sultanahmet, Beyoğlu, Galata and Tophane today. This photo captures the Saliha Sultan Fountain in Galata.

06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.name: Alexandria: The Consuls’ Square Rebuilt
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.author: Patrizia Pampana, Giulia Barrera
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.archival: Licurgo Santoni, *Alto Egitto e Nubia*, Roma, Modes e Mendei, 1905.
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.second_name: The Consuls' Square in Alexandria (Egypt) rebuilt after being destroyed by a fire in 1882
06eab576-316a-57c3-8710-45a77c94f15b.description2: The large, rectangular square initially know under the French name “Place des Consuls” (later as Muhammad 'Ali Square), was officially inaugurated in 1860. It was designed by Francesco Mancini, chief engineer of the “Commissione d’ornato” (Board of Works), a committee set up in 1834 by Muhammad 'Ali (ruler of Egypt in 1805-1848), and modelled after similar urban-planning committees already functioning in some Italian cities. In 1872, an equestrian statue of Muhammad 'Ali was erected in the square, which took his name. In July 1882, after anti-foreign rioting in Alexandria, the British fleet heavily bombed the city, causing major destructions to the buildings surrounding the square.

en: Ghoneim, Mohamed, “Alexandrian Culture in Modern Times: Egyptian Identity and Cosmopolitan Aspects”, in Kenneth Hamma (ed.), *Alexandria and Alexandrianism*, Malibu, CA: J. Paul Getty Museum, 1996: 285–301.

Re, Lucia, “Alexandria Revisited: Colonialism and the Egyptian Works of Enrico Pea and Giuseppe Ungaretti”, in Patrizia Palumbo (ed.), *A Place in the Sun: Africa in Italian Colonial Culture from Post-unification to the Present*, Berkeley, CA: University of California Press, 2003: 163–96.

0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.name: Unicellular House: 'Kukh'
0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.description: This kind of habitation provides only the most basic functions of a house: shelter and warmth. It has no outdoor spaces, and the windows and doors are generally very small. Even today, domestic or social activities (such as cooking, washing, eating, relaxing, working or receiving guests) in these houses generally take place outdoors, either outside the front door or to the side of the house under a canopy or in the shade of a tree. The interior was not divided in any particular way, and divisions between rooms were traditionally created my movable objects, such as cabinets, curtains or wooden partitions. In the *kukh*s of today, solid walls have taken their place.
0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.author: Jeff El-Msanne, David Andos
0789647b-9e7e-5620-892e-044eb391df8f.history: The *kukh* is a modest house. It was the basic model for a traditional house in the agricultural suburbs of Beirut. *Kukh*s were popular until the mid-19th century and were generally inhabited by farmers and their families. They also functioned as temporary shelter for livestock or domestic animals.

078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.name: *Bayt Niyadu, Damascus*
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.second_name: Inhabitants in the courtyard demonstrating the new style of decoration and clothing
078cfe51-b4db-5203-b6c8-54fede56f98d.description2: Like the Lisbuna House, Bayt Niyadu saw two major construction phases, namely, in the 18th and late 19th century. It was refurbished as so many houses between 1865 and 1872 and features marble ornamentation similar to the one in Bayt Lisbuna´s courtyard. These houses are from the layout typical "traditional" courtyard houses of the region. However, the Niyadu House became known (also on postcards) for its richness and abundance of up to date Ottoman decor. The owners expressed their Damascene modernity proudly to the outside – also in this picture: the gentlemen sports a European-style dinner jacket and the lady a mid-length skirt, teamed with a withe blouse in the latest fashion. This transformation of private forms of urban live – notice also the brand new and modern electrical lightening in the "traditional" courtyard – can be seen throughout the city and is an important example of a local expression of global modernity.

0945f0d0-17e6-52da-8c82-4b26290bbf1b.name: Tile panel 'The Threshing of Wheat'
0945f0d0-17e6-52da-8c82-4b26290bbf1b.author: DGPC
0945f0d0-17e6-52da-8c82-4b26290bbf1b.description2: This tile panel depicting the treshing of wheat using animals originally covered the wall of a bakery in Lisbon. Although it reproduces a traditional technique, this tile panel exemplifies the need for modernization of stores and public buildings which took place in main cities throughout Portugal by the beginning of the 20th century.

0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.name: Rossio Railway Station
0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.history: Rossio railway station, commissioned by Conselho Superior de Obras Púbicas was designed in 1886-87 by Portuguese architect José Luís Monteiro. It was built in Rossio, a central and busy square of Lisbon Downtown. A tunnel was excavated under the city and is considered one of the most important works of engineering in Portugal dating from the 19th century; it was completed in 1890.
0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.keywords: Lisbon; Architecture; Romantic Style; Iberian Arab memory; railway station
0a4f03ff-bf1b-52e6-aede-b7826456b1d7.description2: Rossio railway station (Lisbon) was designed by the Portuguese architect José Luís Monteiro. The construction begun in 1886 and was inaugurated on 23 November of 1890. Located in the historical center of Lisbon, the Rossio Station follows the Neo-Manueline architectural style, and is an important Lisbon building of the late Romantic style  from the 19th century.

0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.name: Passengers and onlookers waiting for the métropolitain at the Place de Bastille
0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.second_name: Taken from *Vie et Métiers à Paris*
0c0afba6-5d14-5078-bcea-d6d65921461c.description2: Eugène Atget (1857–1927) began developing an interest in photography in 1888. He created his photos in series, and sold them to institutions. It was thus, that around 1898, he came to photograph the old neighbourhoods of Paris destined to demolition, and sold these photographs to the new Commission du Vieux Paris. As he photographed roads dug up by the urban excavations, he also captured onlookers fascinated by this new mode of transport. The Bastille station is pictured here, one of the overground sections of the ligne 1, which explains how these people were able to comfortably observe. The Colonne de Juillet of the Place de Bastille is visible in the background.

0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.name: Bab Boujloud
0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.history: Bab Boujloud was built in the 12th century and has been restored and refurbished several times since. In 1913, during the reign of Sultan Mulay al-Hafiz, the gate was redecorated in glazed ceramic, blue on the side facing the Old *Medina* and green on the other side. The gate provides a monumental entrance to the square of the same name, west of the Old *Medina* of Fez.
0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.keywords: Portal; Moroccan city; traditional city; Islamic city; urban planning; national identity; traditional space; public space; urban space; plan; urban planning; geometrical motifs; Moroccan architects; Islamic art; Islamic architecture; Islamic influence; Islamic architecture in Morocco
0c2ced6e-dded-579f-8d98-8cd12c83980d.description2: This impressive 12th-century Gate, restored in 1912, is adorned with blue and green ceramic tiling bearing the name of the location. Beyond the aperture of the gate and around it, the landscape stretches over a vast, nearly flat, and irregular area. This area, surrounded by high adobe walls pierced with several doors, holds the prestigious Mulay Idris High School. Place Boujloud is in a strategic position of great cultural importance and very much animated by its popular character. The portal, admired for its fine interlacing ornamentation of blue and green, consists of a central arch and two smaller side arches that are in very good condition.

0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.name: Hotel Kadri
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.description: Both the interior and exterior of the hotel are excellent examples Zahle's traditional stone architecture. It is one of the largest and most luxurious hotels in the city, and is frequently used by officials and dignitaries.
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.history: The Kadri Hotel was built in 1906, and has borne witness to much of the violence and turmoil in modern Lebanon. The hotel was taken over by the Ottoman army in 1914, who used it is a headquarters and hospital during World War I. It was later occupied by Syrian troops and sustained enormous damage. It was restored to its former glory following an extensive restoration project in the mid 90s. The hotel was briefly closed between February 2011 and 2013.
0c3d95fc-e6dc-5e76-8a44-96775f35c8c3.keywords: Kadri; Hotel; Zahle; Lebanon; Tourists; Tourism

0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.name: House
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.dates: End of 19th – beginning of the 20th century
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.author: Prof. Petar Namichev (PhD)
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.history: The architectural concept of the 19th century "tower" house in Metochia and Montenegro influenced the development of spatial features of this type of house in Macedonia.
0c5e1fe1-623d-5fde-b48c-d651eff7a4b0.description2: The architecture of the Reka Area does not show many similar characteristics with neighbouring regions but shares common features with houses in some regions in Bulgaria, Albania, and elsewhere. This is a “tower” type of house. The entire three-storey house was built of stone. Thick and massive stone walls and very small windows on the ground floor were constructed for the purpose of safety in turbulent times, as well as for keeping heat inside during cold winters. The walls on the upper storey with slightly bigger windows were plated with wooden laths. The spatial organization of tower-houses in the Reka area share common features with Albanian tower houses regarding the commodity and defence security. The type of tower-house that used to be built in the Reka Area was the creation of the construction *tajfa* of Maksim Krstich.

0ccfaeef-b75e-522c-ba46-eb30b18d6040.name: Pertevniyal Valide Sultan Mosque Complex
0ccfaeef-b75e-522c-ba46-eb30b18d6040.keywords: Women patrons; religious architecture; Orientalism; Gothic; mosque
0ccfaeef-b75e-522c-ba46-eb30b18d6040.description2: The complex was built by Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, wife of Sultan Mahmud II and mother of Sultan Abdülaziz, who was known for her charitable works. It comprises a mosque, a mausoleum, a *sabil* (water dispensary), a fountain, a clock-room and a school. The mosque reflects the characteristics of its period. The square prayer hall covered with a dome is extended with a wide arch to four sides. Mainly Oriental in style, the mosque is lavishly decorated. It was built with an eclectic taste bringing together elements from Gothic, Ottoman, Islamic and Indian arts.

0cdaaac9-facc-525a-b1f1-756e4b6df842.name: Silvio Benigno Crespi and his family in the courtyard of Villa Pia (Villa Crespi), Orta San Giulio (Novara)
0cdaaac9-facc-525a-b1f1-756e4b6df842.author: Ignazio Galella
0cdaaac9-facc-525a-b1f1-756e4b6df842.description2:
Silvio Benigno Crespi was one of the children of Cristoforo Benigno Crespi, the industrialist who built a Moorish-style villa (known as villa Pia or villa Crespi) built on the lake d’Orta.  
This picture was taken in the courtyard of Villa Crespi. It shows Silvio Benigno Crespi (standing, on the right); sitting on the extreme left is his wife Teresa Ghiglieri; at the centre their first-born child Benigno and their other six children.  
The picture gives a hint of the lifestyle of this stock of cultivated, enlightened and successful industrialists.

0df04b1e-0995-5f3a-a767-e848e62c8fbf.name: *The Bridge Carol I*
0df04b1e-0995-5f3a-a767-e848e62c8fbf.description2: The railroad bridge over the Danube that was built between 1890–1895 in South-Eastern Romania shortened the route of the Orient Express, a passenger train meant to connect Paris to Istanbul. The bridge made it possible for the Orient Express to reach Constanţa, a Black Sea port, from where ships went to Istanbul, whereas in the past the journey implied people being ferried on the Danube from Romania to Bulgaria, travelling by train to Varna (a Bulgarian Black Sea port) and then taking a ship to Istanbul. The “Carol I” bridge, which was designed by engineer Anghel Saligny and was at that time the longest in Europe, was inaugurated on 29 September 1895. In his inaugural speech, the king declared that “Romania is now owner of the shortest route between the northern seas and the countries of the Orient”.

0ef1fad2-ddb0-571e-aa44-e858e5b159ac.name: *Die stadt Algier*
0ef1fad2-ddb0-571e-aa44-e858e5b159ac.author: Dalila Orfali
0ef1fad2-ddb0-571e-aa44-e858e5b159ac.description2: According to the historiographer Gabriel Esquer, this illustration was the most detailed view of Algiers available in the 17th century. The artist has accurately mapped out the streets and houses of the city.

0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.name: The Italian Politeama Rossini theatre in Tunis, inaugurated in 1903
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.author: Giulia Barrera
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 67
0f088fa7-47b1-5825-9ada-f45bc3097162.description2:
The Politeama Rossini was built by the construction company of Giuseppe Di Vittorio (a Sicilian who had migrated to Tunisia in 1882); the architect was a Mr. Baron. It could house an audience of 2,500.  
The first Italian theatre in Tunis was the “Teatro Tapia” founded in 1826. Other Italian theatres (such as the “Teatro Italiano” and the “Teatro Paradiso”) and concert halls (“Gran Teatro”, “Teatro Cohen”, etc.) were created in Tunis the following decades.

0fee6c38-84a6-5884-a476-0a33d319a555.name: Old Serail
0fee6c38-84a6-5884-a476-0a33d319a555.description: This Ottoman Serail was constructed in 1850, and is a mix of local and Ottoman architectural styles. The atrium contains an inner garden which is surrounded by arcades. Today, it serves as the city's town hall and is known as the 'Old Serail'.
0fee6c38-84a6-5884-a476-0a33d319a555.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
0fee6c38-84a6-5884-a476-0a33d319a555.history: The Serail was used as a prison in the past, which suffered of severe overcrowding. The prison was transferred to a larger site in 2009. Today, it functions as a town hall and houses the offices of the municipality, as well as a museum of the city's history.

10420cae-bec5-5219-ac37-b2d0536040b3.name: Hindu Villa
10420cae-bec5-5219-ac37-b2d0536040b3.holder: Ministry of Antiquities; Ministry of Culture
10420cae-bec5-5219-ac37-b2d0536040b3.author: Ahmad al-Bindari
10420cae-bec5-5219-ac37-b2d0536040b3.history: Baron Empain had a passion for stylistic architecture from different parts of the world. The earlier buildings of Heliopolis were a melange of European and Arab architecture at a time when eclecticism was booming in Europe. His Hindu palace was and is still the crown jewel of the buildings of Heliopolis. The Baron Empain Palace was built using an innovative technique called the Hennebique system – named after the French engineer François Hennebique – wherein reinforced concrete was used for the first time. The varied external elements drawn by Marcel were cast in France via the Hennebique enterprise, then transported to Cairo and assembled on-site. The villa’s interior decorations were made by the French interior designer Georges-Louis Claude (1879–1963).
10420cae-bec5-5219-ac37-b2d0536040b3.keywords: Hindu Palace; Baron Empain Palace; Baron Palace; Cambodian Architecture in Cairo
10420cae-bec5-5219-ac37-b2d0536040b3.architects: Architect: Alexandre Marcel; interior designer: Georges-Louis Claude
10420cae-bec5-5219-ac37-b2d0536040b3.description2: The Hindu Villa of the Baron Empain (Edward Louis Joseph Empain, born on 20 September 1852 at Boleil-en-Hainaut, Belgium, died on 22 July 1929 at Waluwe-Saint-Pierre) is known today as the Baron Palace. The house was erected in 1906 following the plans of the French architect Alexandre Marcel (1860–1928), member at the Institut de France. The house reflects a mix of styles: Indian, Mongolian and Chinese, with some Islamic features. The eye-catching silhouette of the palace recalls the image of a Hindu temple. Marcel was already well-known for his exotic opera, in which he merged his masterpieces in a model titled “Panorama around the World: a Japanese Pagoda, Chinese Pavilion and an Indian Temple” that he made for the *Exposition Universelle* in Paris in 1900. This was Marcel’s inspiration for Empain’s residence.

10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.name: Lisbon Botanical Garden
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.type: Botanical Garden; National Monument (Decree nº18/2010, DR, nº250  28  December 2010)
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.dates: Starting of plantation: 1873; opened to the public: 1878; belongs to the University of Lisbon since 1911
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.author: Catarina Teixeira (MUHNAC-UL), David Felismino (MUHNAC-UL)
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.history: Since its creation in 1837, the Polytechnic School is committed to use  the Botanical Garden to support teaching and research in Botany. This purpose was firstly achieved at the Royal Botanical Garden at Ajuda, whose scientific and administrative supervision passed to the Polytechnic School in 1839. The installation of the new garden begins in 1873, on the initiative of Conde de Ficalho (1837–1903), and it opens to the public in 1878. In the 20th century, a new Herbarium building was added (1942) and, in 1962, a new Greenhouse replacing the original one, degraded by use and by the bombings of 1927. Topographically the Botanic Garden consists of two distinct parts – a flat area, dedicated to systematic botany and a gentle slope with the collection of trees and shrubs (Arboretum).
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.keywords: Botanical Garden; Collections; National Museum of Natural History and Science; Polytechnic School
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.architects: Ordered by Manuel Melo Breyner, Conde de Ficalho (1837–1903). Author of the design and arrangement of the Order Beds: German botanist Goeze Edmund (1838–1929), Arboretum: French botanist Jules Daveau (1852–1929)
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.second_name: Botanical Garden of the University of Lisbon
10a5b375-34b0-5c68-bd08-21bc738e5e36.description2: The Garden holds more than 1,500 specimens over 4 acres, highlighting a remarkable diversity of palms and a unique collection of Cycadaceae, with exemplars only surviving in some parts of the world. It is also rich in species from New Zealand, Australia, China, Japan and South America, demonstrating the peculiarities of different microclimates created by its topography. The Garden fulfils also national requirements, both by the universality of its collection, and by the quality and quantity of the associated collections (herbaria, wood collections, seed bank). Furthermore, it includes relevant edified heritage, designed by important Portuguese architects from the 19th and 20th centuries.

10eff4e6-77c9-5f30-9f3f-98be6f9c668a.description2: It is a residence that was built by Sultan Abdulhamid II for resting in Hasbahche. 113d81d8-ec2d-5435-9b8d-e7c59e9ff9fb.name: The Ghetto of Florence
113d81d8-ec2d-5435-9b8d-e7c59e9ff9fb.author: Marina Minozzi
113d81d8-ec2d-5435-9b8d-e7c59e9ff9fb.keywords: Macchiaioli; Italian painters; painting; artistic exchanges; Corot; landscape; cityscape; realism; unification of Italy; social history; social topics; Italian society; post-unitarian Italian society; Italian Jews; city; urban space; segregation; ghetto
113d81d8-ec2d-5435-9b8d-e7c59e9ff9fb.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
113d81d8-ec2d-5435-9b8d-e7c59e9ff9fb.description2: Telemaco Signorini was part of the group of artists known as The Macchiaioli Movement, a group drawn to colour and nature. After his studies at the Academy of Florence, he started painting from real life and spent some time in Paris, where he met Corot and the painters from the School of Barbizon. Back in Italy the artist went to Tuscany and Liguria. He also travelled frequently to France, England and Scotland, where he was well known. Signorini liked painting urban scenes and cityscapes. The artist developed urban themes with a unique emphasis, matching together vivid descriptions, social and humanitarian features and cultural issues.

138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.name: *View of Constantinople*
138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.author: Papastratos 1990, vol. 2, 578-79, figs. 617-18; Delivorrias, Fotopoulos 1997, 508-9, figs. 900-901
138b0748-bba7-544a-afa4-6e44661538d4.description2: Both this print and the *View of Smyrna* are based on earlier Western ones, which have been assimilated into the distinctive Athonite topographical style. They are exceptions to the corpus of Athonite prints, since they are of secular subjects. The printmaker was, indeed, active outside Athos, where he executed nonreligious commissions. The subjects relate to the tradition of topographical murals depicting important commercial and cultural centers of the day that decorated the mansions of wealthy merchants by the mid-eighteenth century. Kaldis aimed to supply a wider public with inexpensive works of a decorative nature. The activity of merchants from Lesbos at Smyrna, Constantinople, and the Black Sea on the one hand justified the choice of subject and, on the other, provided the appropriate network in which the multiple printed works could circulate. In order to attract the largest possible clientele, the view is coloured and annotated with explanatory comments in Greek and Turkish.

14597b52-b897-5eac-9ab6-b73b6fabbf11.name: House
14597b52-b897-5eac-9ab6-b73b6fabbf11.dates: End of 19th – beginning of the 20th century
14597b52-b897-5eac-9ab6-b73b6fabbf11.author: Prof. Petar Namichev (PhD)
14597b52-b897-5eac-9ab6-b73b6fabbf11.history: The first mention of the Debar-Reka art school in the sources was in the 10th century. The centre of the art school was in the village of Galichnik. Activities of the Debar-Galichnik art centre throughout the centuries have given rise to the development of diverse crafts related to construction and architectural decoration, as well as icon-painting, woodcarving, sculpture, etc. The male population of the Reka area was traditionally widely known for their construction skills. These native architects used to work in groups called *tajfas*. *Tajfas* consisted of around ten men, including builders, wood-carving masters and stone cutters. The leader of the *tajfa*, i.e. the person that used to organize the construction activities, was called *ustabashiya*.
14597b52-b897-5eac-9ab6-b73b6fabbf11.description2: The existence of structures with similar architectonic features in the Reka Area, the territory of Metochia, Albania, Greece, Bulgaria and Bosnia confirms the common concept of expression in dwellings of "tower" type in the traditional architecture of the Balkans. This three-storey house of symmetrical layout is built of stone. It shows some features of tower-houses with its very small windows built extremely high at the ground floor and symmetrically positioned bigger windows on upper stories. The house is distinguished by the interesting entrance portion.

147c8e1e-4cb1-51c6-a42b-c10e8b602904.name: Tender specification relating to the supply of running water to Tangier
147c8e1e-4cb1-51c6-a42b-c10e8b602904.description: The Chérifien government established 34 specifications altogether listing the causes and conditions for adjudication in order to supply the city of Tangier with a reliable, abundant water supply.
147c8e1e-4cb1-51c6-a42b-c10e8b602904.keywords: Modernisation; Moroccan society; city; urban spaces; Moroccan city; water supply; reforms; social changes; health; hygiene; water management

14fdce8b-d60e-5d32-ad42-c489568e4c66.name: Collective housing
14fdce8b-d60e-5d32-ad42-c489568e4c66.description: This type of collective housing, which was popular until the mid-19th century, generally consisted of houses built in sandstone or limestone *ramleh*, covered by a cray terrace and reinforced concrete slabs. The plan of the house is built around a central courtyard.
14fdce8b-d60e-5d32-ad42-c489568e4c66.author: Jeff El-Msanne, David Andos
14fdce8b-d60e-5d32-ad42-c489568e4c66.history: A *hawsh* is a style of collective housing built around a *harat* (an Arabic term which literally means "lane"). It consists of several main buildings built around a common courtyard, which were usually occupied by families or relatives of similar geographical origins. Unlike the *dar* (another type of house built around a central courtyard), there is no hierarchy in the distribution of the buildings around the courtyard. In the suburb of Medwwar-Rmeil, Beirut, Beirut, an area which in the 19th century relied mostly on the agricultural sector, the *hawsh* was typically leased to the newly installed peasant families.

1ac5c099-15f5-5bc0-b9bd-13a0de13ed0b.name: Al-Majidiyya Mosque
1ac5c099-15f5-5bc0-b9bd-13a0de13ed0b.description: Located by the coast, north of Beirut's downtown, al-Majidiyya Mosque was once an 18th century Ottoman defensive fort.
1ac5c099-15f5-5bc0-b9bd-13a0de13ed0b.author: Jeff El-Msanne
1ac5c099-15f5-5bc0-b9bd-13a0de13ed0b.history: In 1841, this ex-Ottoman fort was turned into a mosque and named after the Ottoman sultan 'Abd al-Majid I. The mosque was then enlarged and renovated in 1881 and in 1906. Its tall, pencil-shaped minaret is built in the typical Ottoman style, whereas the shorter minaret resembles the Beiruti-Mamluk style. The interior of the mosque has conserved the arches and vaulted ceilings of the Ottoman fort it once was.

1aee0242-efb1-5288-9004-18c010d1d030.name: *Raqqi Synagogue, Damascus*
1aee0242-efb1-5288-9004-18c010d1d030.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
1aee0242-efb1-5288-9004-18c010d1d030.author: Stefan Weber
1aee0242-efb1-5288-9004-18c010d1d030.second_name: Courtyard, demonstrating the architectural vicinity to dwellings
1aee0242-efb1-5288-9004-18c010d1d030.description2: The Raqqi Synagogue is a basalt construction from the late 19th century in Damascus. It was one of the several synagogues in the city, all of them built or rebuilt in the 19th century. Thus, the are relatively new in comparison to the long history of Jews in city. Its architectural style and decoration is very close to urban dwellings of the period. In 2011, extensive renovation plans for this important synagogue were passed.

1ccb2e38-9e35-5e04-be15-39d7faa20cc7.name: Bahiya Palace
1ccb2e38-9e35-5e04-be15-39d7faa20cc7.history: The site of the palace lies southeast of the Marrakesh *Medina*, close to the present royal palace. It was built in two phases by a father and son who served as grand viziers to two ‘Alawid sultans. The first part of the palace, known as Dar Si Musa ‒ the largest and most luxurious in Morocco at the time ‒ was built between 1866 and 1867 by Si Musa, grand vizier to Sultan Muhammad ibn ‘Abd al-Rahman (reigned 1859-73). Between 1894 and 1900, the second phase of construction started under Si Musa’s son, Si Ahmad ibn Musa, grand vizier to two sultans Mulay al-Hasan I (1873-94) and Mulay ‘Abd al-‘Aziz (1894-1908), to designs by the architect Muhammad ibn Makki al-Misfiwi. During his reign, Ahmad ibn Musa enlarged the southern part of his father’s palace and subsequently developed a number of glamorously designed connecting houses. He lived on the grounds with four wives, a harem of 24 official concubines and their many children. Having built the palace for his favourite wife, Ahmad ibn Musa named it *Bahiya*, meaning “beautiful, brilliant”.
1ccb2e38-9e35-5e04-be15-39d7faa20cc7.keywords: Islamic art; Islamic architecture; Islamic architecture in Morocco; Moroccan architects; traditional city; Islamic city; palace; royal palace; plan; urban planning; stucco; garden; patio; Islamic garden; zellij; ceramic; geometrical motifs; gardens and architecture
1ccb2e38-9e35-5e04-be15-39d7faa20cc7.description2: Covering an area of eight hectares, the palace consists of 150 rooms lavishly decorated with *mashrabiyya*, marble sculptures, paintings on beech and cedar, stuccowork and *zellige*. Built in two phases in the second half of the 19th century, the estate is comprised of structures built piecemeal, including outbuildings and ancillary structures: a Turkish bath, mosque and stables, and other annexed houses that are connected to each other, many of which are remarkable both in their structure and their ornamentation. Although the buildings are arranged disparately throughout the estate they are organised around several patios and green Islamic-style gardens (*al-agdal*), planted with orange, banana and cypress trees, as well as hibiscus and jasmine, and irrigated by *qanat*.

1e164505-7b44-5ab0-8ab5-124407905064.name: Model of the brig *Mariţa*
1e164505-7b44-5ab0-8ab5-124407905064.description2: In 1834 Wallachia and Moldavia, which were under Ottoman suzerainty, were granted by the Ottoman Empire the right to sail on the Danube using their national banners. The first Romanian ship to sail under Romanian banner was the brig “Marița”, built in the naval dockyard of the Giurgiu port. Its owner was Wallachian politician Alexandru Vilara, who gave it the name of the wife of Alexandru II Ghica, Wallachia’s ruler between 1834-1842. “Marița” began its first trip in December 1834. Its destination was Istanbul, where it transported 300 kg of wheat. It returned in June 1835 after having been seriously damaged by two storms, one of which on its way back, when the crew had to throw overboard the wine purchased from Istanbul.

1f9cc409-36e4-51f2-828e-77a94d820a08.name: Istanbul water pipeline map
1f9cc409-36e4-51f2-828e-77a94d820a08.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
1f9cc409-36e4-51f2-828e-77a94d820a08.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; History of Water in Ottoman Empire; Water; map
1f9cc409-36e4-51f2-828e-77a94d820a08.description2: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. The Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902. The station is located at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique reminder of Ottoman architecture. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – with water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane, propelled by steam pump machines.

1fa42ca0-8bff-5098-bc57-bbb59a4fe4bf.name: Monastery of St. George – Rajchica
1fa42ca0-8bff-5098-bc57-bbb59a4fe4bf.author: Darko Nikolovski
1fa42ca0-8bff-5098-bc57-bbb59a4fe4bf.history: The Church was built in 1835. Upper zones of its frescoes were painted in the span of 1840–1852 by icon-painter Mihail and priest Danail. Lower zones were completed by their disciple, the renowned icon-painter Dicho Zograph from v. Tresonche near Debar, one of the most outstanding Macedonian icon painters.
1fa42ca0-8bff-5098-bc57-bbb59a4fe4bf.architects: Local construction masters. Frescoes painted by icon painter Mihail, monk Daniel and their student Dicho Zograph
1fa42ca0-8bff-5098-bc57-bbb59a4fe4bf.description2: The Monastery in v. Rajchica near Debar is one of the most outstanding 19th-century monasteries in the Republic of Macedonia. The Monastery Church is dedicated to St. George Victorious. It is a model of sacral structure distinctive of the 19th century local construction masters from the Reka Area. The church is a combination of inscribed cross and single-nave structure with three domes. Part of the holy remains of St. George the Victorious – that is, his hand – is kept in the monastery. For many years now the monastery has been serving as a nunnery and nuns have been creating and embroidering robes for church dignitaries in Macedonia and elsewhere.

21301784-a7a9-5271-b156-37a91e6af337.name: Ma'an Railway Station
21301784-a7a9-5271-b156-37a91e6af337.author: Mohammad Najjar
21301784-a7a9-5271-b156-37a91e6af337.history: In 1900-1908, Sultan Abdul Hamid with the help and support of Germany established a Railway between Damascus and Mecca (1700 km) to facilitate transporting the pilgrims. The track from Medina to Mecca (400 km) was never realized. The cost of the project was estimated at approximately 5 million Ottoman golden liras, which were provided from: private donations, revenues of the Ottoman State from the sale of stamps, and a special tax upon all citizens for the railway. Construction of the narrow-gauge track (105cm) began in 1900 with a wire telegraph line along its side connecting Damascus with Medina across Amman with a total track length of 1303 km. Official inaugurations of the tracks and stations were scheduled to coincide with the accession of the Sultan to the throne in the month of September every year. The construction of the project ended in 1908.
21301784-a7a9-5271-b156-37a91e6af337.keywords: Hijaz; railway; station; pilgrimage; hajj; pilgrimage route; communication; telegraph; Jordan; Damascus; Mecca; Makka; Amman; Zarqa; Qatranah; Ma'an; Amman; Tabuk; Arabian Peninsula; Ottoman; Abd al Hamid; Germany; Meinsner
21301784-a7a9-5271-b156-37a91e6af337.description2: Ma'an station was one of the most important stations along the Hijaz railway. It consists of several buildings parallel to the railway that include a passengers' hall, maintenance workshops, water towers and the residence of the German engineer Meinsner who was in charge for the construction of the Hijaz railway. With its various components including the rails, steam engines, bridges and stations, the project stands as an industrial, architectural and engineering statement that had a huge influence on Jordan. The Amman-Ma'an Section was completed in September 1904. The Ma'an-Tabuk Section was completed in September 1906.

21cf7fa5-ac97-5097-8b52-ba4324bd02bd.name: Edward Dodwell, *View in Greece* (London 1830)
21cf7fa5-ac97-5097-8b52-ba4324bd02bd.description2: Edward Dodwell recorded the trasformation of the ancient Tower of the Winds into a dervish teke and in the early 19th century it wqas particularly popular with the travellers. Scenes from the city of Athens. Over the lintel, which faces the north-east, upon a red ground, is inscribed the Arabic *La Illah, Allah, Mahamed u resoul ullah* declaring there to be no God but God, and Muhammad to be his prophet. The wooden floor of the interior rests upon the lower cornice, many feet above the ancient pavement. The marble walls are washed with a uniform white. The *mihrab*, painted in perpendicular stripes of green and red, indicates by its position the direction of the Kaaba, or oratory of Mecca; each side of this is a wax candle, and the green flag of the prophet has also its place. The Qur'an is deposited within this niche, and an imitation of the two-edged sword of 'Ali is attached to the adjoining wall. Before these is performed the circularly whirling dance of the Dervishes, witnessing which, the spectator will find it as difficult to remain serious, as it would be dangerous to appear otherwise.

21dee5ec-7459-5915-8d20-a2fe4b38d5d8.name: Yıldız Palace State Apartments Kiosk
21dee5ec-7459-5915-8d20-a2fe4b38d5d8.notice: This is an unedited Database entry and may contain errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are working to raise the funds required to complete the editing; should you wish to contribute please visit our [Support page](https://www.museumwnf.org/atrium_support.php).

Yildiz Palace, which is the last architectural example of Turkish Ottoman palace, is located on the Yildiz hill in the district of Besiktas. Sultan Ahmed I was the first to build a pavilion, over this land registered at the time to the Private treasury of the Ottoman Sultan as a hunting place sultans beginning during the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566).  
The main construction in the palace started in the period of Sultan Abdulhamid II (1876-1909) and it was called Saray-i Humayun (Central palace). During this period the palace comprised of buildings for private use of the sultan as well as buildings, allocated for the officials, repair shops and carpentry like repairing shop, carpenter’s shop and the buildings of culture and art such as theatre, museum and library. The Palace begun to serve as a museum under the name of “Directorate of the Museum of Yildiz Palace since 1993.
21dee5ec-7459-5915-8d20-a2fe4b38d5d8.architects: Balyan family – Sarkis Balyan (1835, Istanbul – 1899, Istanbul)
21dee5ec-7459-5915-8d20-a2fe4b38d5d8.description2: This is the most magnificent kiosk of the palace. It was commissioned by Sultan Abdulaziz in 1866 and built by the architects of Balyan family. The exterior siding of the kiosk is decorated with fluted and composite capitals, columns, corbel and sectional architraves. The inner plan of the kiosk is based on the old architectural tradition. It is famous with the Divanhane with pool downstairs and the stairs with the crystal handrails to the second floor. While the upper floor was used by the sultan, other sections were used by senior officials of the palace. Ghazi Osman Pasha, Commander of Plevne War served as Marshal of the Court in this building. Having served as the administration headquarters of the state during the reign of Sultan Abdulhamid II (1876-1909), the kiosk was used for important receptions and feasts both in the Ottoman Empire and after the Declaration of the Republic.

229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.name: Beirut Railway Station
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.description: This railway station, built during the Ottoman period, was the first railway station in Lebanon. It was a public station, intended for both for the transportation of passengers and trading goods.
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.history: The Beirut-Damascus railway line, opened in 1895, was built across mountainous terrain to a 1,050 mm gauge. The second line from Riyaq to Aleppo, via Lebanon's eastern Beqaa valley, was also approved around this time. This was built to a standard gauge, even though it was only intended to provide a service between Damascus and Aleppo. The northern city of Tripoli was also connected via railway to Homs.
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.keywords: Commerce; Train station; Railway; Transportation; Trading
229065fa-d12d-59dd-89b0-038e40916456.architects: “Société des chemins de fer Ottomans économique de Beyrouth-damas-Hauran”

23d98ad7-7f2d-5f3d-a18a-862042cf2b0c.name: The Ottoman Clock Tower
23d98ad7-7f2d-5f3d-a18a-862042cf2b0c.author: Julien El Khoury, Jeff El-Msanne
23d98ad7-7f2d-5f3d-a18a-862042cf2b0c.history: This clock tower was built by Yussef Afimus in 1897 neara the Grand Serail to celebrate the 10th anniversary of the Ottoman sultan 'Abd al-Hamid II's coronation. It was seen as an important tower, indicating Muslim prayer time as well as making up for the absence of a public clock tower in the city, as many private foreign institutions in Beirut had built Western style clock towers in recent years. The construction of the clock tower was approved by the sultan following a letter of supplication from Beirut's governor Rashid Bey. The ceremonial laying of the first stone took place on 9 January 1897 (the anniversary of the sultan) in the presence of high officials, military representatives and members of the municipality of Beirut.
23d98ad7-7f2d-5f3d-a18a-862042cf2b0c.description2: At 25 metres tall, the Hamidiye clock tower was the tallest structure in Beirut at the time of its completion. Similar towers were consequently built in imitation in numerous other cities of the Ottoman Empire, such as Istanbul, Izmir, Izmit, Adana, Jaffa, Nablus, Acre and Tripoli. It was built using local stone: Beirut sandstone, Jounieh limestone, Damascene basalt and Deir al-Qamar red stone. The tower houses a huge bell weighing 300kg on its third floor, and a set of 125 cast iron steps leading up to it. Four miniature orientalist-style balconies adorn this floor. Above these balconies are four large clock faces imported especially from the Ottoman embassy in France.

257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.name: Postcard of Khan Antoun Bey Square
257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.keywords: Postcard; Khan; Souk; Trade; Economy; Beirut
257442d0-cc8b-5f59-9bdf-31aeac1cd79c.description2: Located next to the port, the Khan Antoun Bey Square was the entrance to the city for those arriving by sea. By the 19th century the *khan* itself, pictured here, housed trading offices on the ground and first floors and foreign consulates on the upper floors. The inner courtyard was used to park the consuls' horse-drawn carriages.

2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.name: The Great Mosque and University of Zaytuna
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.history: Located in the heart of the Tunis medina, the great Zaytuna Mosque is the largest and most revered religious site in Tunis. City life revolved around this mosque, as it was not only an important place of worship, but also a great university, with a reputation matching that of the Qaraouyine University in Fez and the al-Azhar University in Cairo. Many theologians and scholars of literature, arts and sciences were trained here for generations. Although it was the subject of many reforms in the 19th century, the modern Zaytuna University still provides a religious education, and attracts many believers at prayer times.
2669ff94-bd70-55d1-a06b-cc0cbefd980d.description2: An important place of worship, the Zaytuna mosque was subject to a great number of adjustments and expansions since its construction in the 7th century, most notably during the 17th and 18th centuries. The central courtyard is accessible through a suspended portico with horseshoe archways resting on beautiful columns topped with Hafsid capitals, through which the beautiful painted wooden ceilings can be seen. The paved courtyard is dominated by a square minaret, a beautiful sundial and a ribbed calotte which rests on an octagonal base above on a larger, square base. The décor is reminiscent of the Dome of the Rock in al-Quds (Jerusalem) in Palestine.

2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.name: Outline map of Damascus in 1918
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.author: Stefan Weber
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.second_name: Indicating urban growth to the fin de siecle
2711a503-9f23-5282-b34a-bc7b254979eb.description2: Damascus, now the political and cultural centre of Syria, is one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities. The design of its living spaces and the organization of urban society were always connected to the culture of its inhabitants. Damascus’ geographical space reflects this “spatial turn”: Its public spaces were clearly shaped and influenced by the diverse social, historical and cultural structures and events, which contributed to the vitality of Damascus’ multilayered Urban Design.

275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.name: Yıldız Tile Imperial Factory
275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; Ancient Istanbul; yıldız tile; ceramic; factories
275bf73d-6170-5205-804c-fbb1ff637342.description2: The Yıldız Tile Imperial Factory was founded by Sultan Abdülhamid II (1876-1909) in the early 1890’s in the garden of Yıldız Palace for the purposes of arousing, reshaping and stimulating the Turkish tiling art. The factory, which began manufacturing immediately, was damaged in the earthquake of 1894 and in the same year, it was nearly reconstructed by Italian Architect Raimondo d’Aronco.

27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.name: Lisbon Astronomical Observatory
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.holder: National Museum of Natural History and Science (MUHNAC) / Museums of the University of Lisbon
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.author: António Perestrelo de Matos (MUHNAC-UL), Marta C. Lourenço (MUHNAC-UL)
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.history: The Observatory was constructed with the support and sponsorship of King Pedro V (1837–1861). It began operating in 1867 and its first director was Frederico Oom, followed by Campos Rodrigues (1836–1919), an internationally recognised astronomer and a creator of several scientific instruments. In 1995, the Observatory integrated the University of Lisbon.
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.keywords: Observatory; Scientific Heritage; Astronomy; National Museum of Natural History and Science; University of Lisbon
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.architects: Architects: Jean François Gille Colson, José da Costa Sequeira (1800–1872), Valentim José Correia (1822–1900); Engineer: Frederico Augusto Oom (1830–1890)
27b52e92-40ef-53b5-9de2-ba320998fdf0.description2: The Lisbon Astronomical Observatory is the Portuguese national observatory. It has the legal responsibility of national timekeeping. It is located in the Tapada da Ajuda, a green area in the west of Lisbon. It is part of the Museums of the University of Lisbon/National Museum of Natural History and Science. It includes several buildings. It promotes activities regarding the public understanding of astronomy and astrophysics for diverse audiences. The Observatory has important collections: scientific instruments, mostly from the 19th and early 20th century; a Library, which is reference in Portugal, and an important historical archive.

27bffbe0-bf77-51b6-87f3-1667b65ae607.name: *The Ruins of the Temple of the Sun at Baalbec*
27bffbe0-bf77-51b6-87f3-1667b65ae607.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
27bffbe0-bf77-51b6-87f3-1667b65ae607.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
27bffbe0-bf77-51b6-87f3-1667b65ae607.description2: This dramatic view looks across the great court of the temple complex in Baalbek. In the ancient world Baalbek, to the east of Beirut in Lebanon, was a great centre of trade between Europe and Asias, and home to a religion of sun worship. The Scottish artist David Roberts visited in 1839 and over the following years made many images of the still imposing ruins. This painting is Roberts's last of Baalbek, and he considered it as 'a grand finale' to his career as a painter of the Middle East. The complex's imposing architectural and artistic details also inspired European Neoclassical architects and artists such as Robert Adam. Since about 1864 many tourists visited the famed site, including, in 1898, the German emperor Wilhelm II on his way to Jerusalem. Struck by the magnificence of the ruins, he dispatched a German archaeological team, whose subsequent work resulted in a meticulously presented and illustrated publication that further raised interest in Baalbek.

27d99320-2ed8-57cc-b76a-ed939f64f812.name: St George Greek Orthodox Cathedral
27d99320-2ed8-57cc-b76a-ed939f64f812.description: The Cathedral's main plan is rectangular, and approximately 30 metres long by 20 metres wide. The nave itself is 30 metres long by 7.5 metres wide and is subdivided into five bays, which are then subdivided into three aisles. These aisles are divided by eight impressive sandstone piers measuring approximately 8.5 metres in height, with square divisions, chamfered sides and protruding bases. The central aisle is a barrel vault intersected by a vaulted transept. Light which filters through the upper windows shines on the frescoes which cover the vaulted ceiling. The cathedral has three altar spaces, built into three semi-circular alcoves. Finally, the cathedral is most famous for the half-vaulted painted dome above the central apse, in the central aisle.
27d99320-2ed8-57cc-b76a-ed939f64f812.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
27d99320-2ed8-57cc-b76a-ed939f64f812.history: The final modifications to the cathedral's structure were completed in 1910, with its enlargement eastwards and westwards, the addition of a vaulted portico on the south facade and moving the bell tower to the south-east corner. The interior of the Church is decorated with frescoes donated by Ibrahim Yussef Saad.
27d99320-2ed8-57cc-b76a-ed939f64f812.keywords: Greek; Orthodox; Church; Cathedral; Religion; Beirut

28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.name: Grand Bazar Arabe. A late-19th-century bazaar built in Tunis by the construction company of G. Di Vittorio, an Italian immigrant in Tunisia
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th century
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.author: Giulia Barrera
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 189
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.third_name: *Grand Bazar Arabe. G. Di Vittorio imprenditore. Tunisi*
28039875-4e38-5259-a55c-6b799bdfae9b.description2:
On the main entrance one can read the shop sign “Grand Bazar Kassar Said”; on the left “Grand Bazar Arab” and on the right, one can read the shop sign “I. Piperno”: Piperno is an unmistakably Italian Jewish name.  
Giuseppe Di Vittorio, who ran the construction company that built this building, migrated from Termini Imerese (a small town near Palermo, Sicily, Italy) in 1882.

283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.name: Dar Jellouli
283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.history: Located in the heart of Sfax medina, the capital of southern Tunisia, Dar Jellouli once belonged to a rich family from the local nobility. Many members of this family had occupied important positions in the Regency's government throughout the modern period. For example, from 1772 to 1782 Baccar Jellouli was the governor of Sfax. His sons Mohamed and Mahmoud were also members of the city's local government. However, the family made much of its fortune through commercial activities, particularly by owning a fleet of privateer ships. This building was the seat of the local government then from 1939 housed the Centre des Arts under the direction of Lucien Golvin. after independence it became the Musée Régional des Arts et Traditions Populaires.
283da928-6b2e-51fe-a9c1-636157c2ae53.description2: With a simple façade and built in a traditional Tunisian style, this house is built around a central square courtyard paved with white marble and with walls covered in blue tiles. The top two storeys are fitted with an ambulatory and wooden railings. The family's wealth is evident from the carved stone framework, ceramics, carved stucco, woodwork, and floors paved with imported marble. The ground floor contains a number of upside-down-T-shaped rooms which attempt to recreate scenes of daily life in 19th century Sfax. The first-floor rooms hold a collection of traditional clothes. Finally, the second floor holds a collection of painting and Arabic calligraphy.

2ab573cd-8e69-51f0-8275-3af031e2fa06.name: *The View of the City of Algiers*
2ab573cd-8e69-51f0-8275-3af031e2fa06.author: Dalila Orfali

2afaee38-c8b6-5f96-881c-e8b6d088c400.name: Amman Railway Station
2afaee38-c8b6-5f96-881c-e8b6d088c400.author: Mohammad Najjar
2afaee38-c8b6-5f96-881c-e8b6d088c400.history: In 1900-1908, Sultan Abdul Hamid with the help and support of Germany established a Railway between Damascus and Mecca (1700 km) to facilitate transporting the pilgrims. The track from Medina to Mecca (400 km) was never realized. The cost of the project was estimated at approximately 5 million Ottoman golden liras, which were provided from: private donations, revenues of the Ottoman State from the sale of stamps, and a special tax upon all citizens for the railway. Construction of the narrow-gauge track (105cm) began in 1900 with a wire telegraph line along its side connecting Damascus with Medina across Amman with a total track length of 1303 km. Official inaugurations of the tracks and stations were scheduled to coincide with the accession of the Sultan to the throne in the month of September every year. The construction of the project ended in 1908.
2afaee38-c8b6-5f96-881c-e8b6d088c400.keywords: Hijaz; railway; station; pilgrimage; hajj; pilgrimage route; communication; telegraph; Jordan; Damascus; Mecca; Makka; Amman; Zarqa; Qatranah; Ma'an; Amman; Tabuk; Arabian Peninsula; Ottoman; Abd al Hamid; Germany; Meinsner
2afaee38-c8b6-5f96-881c-e8b6d088c400.description2: Amman station was one of the main stations on the Hijaz railway. The location of the town of Amman along the Hijaz railroad had become a decisive factor in choosing Amman as the capital city of the Emirate of Transjordan in 1921. The station consists of several buildings including a passengers' waiting hall, maintenance depots and distinctive water towers. The various components of the project including the rails, steam engines, bridges and stations were an industrial, architectural and engineering statement that had a huge influence on Jordan. The Zarqa-Amman Section was completed in September 1903.

2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.name: *Turkish Country Houses on the Bosphorus*
2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.provenance: First published in Julia Pardoe, *The Beauties of the Bosphorus*, London 1838, facing page 40
2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.artist: Drawn by William Henry Bartlett; engraved by J. C. Bentley
2cac8790-8730-5708-8f5a-80058a37752b.description2: This engraving shows the typical, wooden Ottoman yalis or summer houses built along the shores of the Bosphorus by high-ranking officials and members of the elite since the late 17th century. Designed to reflect both their location, making maximum use of the waterfront, and the taste and status of their owner, the yalis provided a welcome and comfortable escape from the congested city. Their interior, with separate areas for public reception and private family quarters, was furnished, with inbuilt cupboards and diwans, and decorated in the traditional Ottoman style. Only in the 19th century were aspects of European-style interior design and furniture adopted widely. The facades of the yalis were traditionally painted a deep rose colour, until European influence led to the adoption of pastel shades in the 19th century. The image was originally published in Julia Pardoe's 'The Beauties of the Bosphorus', published in London by George Virtue in 1838.

2df6225e-8ea7-5fef-a311-cc29307168e3.name: *Excavation of Samarra*
2df6225e-8ea7-5fef-a311-cc29307168e3.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
2df6225e-8ea7-5fef-a311-cc29307168e3.author: Stefan Weber
2df6225e-8ea7-5fef-a311-cc29307168e3.second_name: Great Mosque with the famous minaret (Malwiya) of the caliphal city of Samarra, groundbreaking excavation by E. Herzfeld 1911–13
2df6225e-8ea7-5fef-a311-cc29307168e3.description2: Of great importance for the collection of the first Museum of Islamic Art in the western world are the findings made during the excavations in Samarra, which were conducted by Ernst Herzfeld and the museum’s first director, Friedrich Sarre, between 1911 and 1913. The study of the Abbasid’s temporal second capital has contributed to an understanding of the developments and changes in Islamic art at the time.

2e86f805-0ac2-5af3-82ca-11820cd27c1d.name: Beaufort Castle
2e86f805-0ac2-5af3-82ca-11820cd27c1d.description: The Beaufort Castle was a crusader castle located near the town of Nabatiyeh, in South Lebanon. The castle was named "Bel Fort" or "Beau Fort" by the Crusaders in the 12th century. Its name in Arabic is *Qal'at al-Shaqiif*, meaning Castle on the High Rock. The castle was also used for military purposes in the 20th century, particularly during the civil war, due to its strategic location.
2e86f805-0ac2-5af3-82ca-11820cd27c1d.author: Julien El Khoury, Jeff El-Msanne
2e86f805-0ac2-5af3-82ca-11820cd27c1d.history: In 1139, King Fulk of Jerusalem gained control of this area and begun the construction of Beaufort castle shortly afterwards. Although Saladin recaptured Beaufort in 1190, the castle was returned to crusader hands only 60 years later. In 1268 Sultan Baybars finally gained control of the fortress. However, the upper portion was destroyed by the Ottomans in the 17th century, as they sought to quash Emir Fakhr al-Din II, who had taken the castle as part of his network of fortifications. Following the Galilee Earthquake in 1837, which caused considerable damage to the structure, the castle was abandoned and its ruins were used by local farmers to shelter sheep, and as a quarry.
2e86f805-0ac2-5af3-82ca-11820cd27c1d.keywords: fortress; castle; tourism; ruins; Beaufort; medieval

301c225c-a1be-58da-b355-55c3b3a1d1e6.name: *A watchman on a Constantinople street*
301c225c-a1be-58da-b355-55c3b3a1d1e6.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
301c225c-a1be-58da-b355-55c3b3a1d1e6.dates: Hegira late 13th – early 14th century / AD late 19th – early 20th century
301c225c-a1be-58da-b355-55c3b3a1d1e6.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
301c225c-a1be-58da-b355-55c3b3a1d1e6.description2: This painting shows an old watchman, carrying his lantern around the old streets of Istanbul. By the times of sultan Abd al-Hamid II (1293 H/1876 CE – 1327 H/1909 CE) the nature of urban life in the Ottoman empire began to change markedly. In Istanbul, Izmir, Edirne, Salonica and other major cities, streets were paved and lit with gas lamps, while horse drawn trams increasingly plied the streets. Political reforms and  new technologies introduced in the13th century H/ 19th century CE gradually transformed Istanbul into a modern international city. Innovative technological achievements such as electric lighting became more and more common, slowly replacing traditionally essential services like those provided by the watchmen of the city, guarding the city quarters with their hand-held lanterns during the hours of darkness.

307c3b5c-a525-55c7-89a1-8342e6da903a.name: Dolmabahçe Palace Imperial Gate
307c3b5c-a525-55c7-89a1-8342e6da903a.keywords: Photograph; Old İstanbul Photograph; İstanbul; James Robertson
307c3b5c-a525-55c7-89a1-8342e6da903a.description2: James Robertson arrived in Istanbul in 1840 and started work as head etcher in Ottoman Mint. He began taking photos of Istanbul soon after. Dolmabahçe Palace was built by Sultan Abdulmecid (1839-1861), who was the thirty first Ottoman Sultan. The palace, whose construction commenced on 13 June 1843, was brought into use on 7 June 1856, upon completion of its surrounding walls. The palace mainly consists of three parts: the Imperial Mabeyn (State Apartments), Muayede Salon (Ceremonial Hall) and the Imperial Harem. Evident Western influences, observed in the style, details and ornaments, are reflections of the aesthetic values as they changed through the last period of the Imperial. On the other hand, it is a building complex in which traditional Turkish House style was applied on a large scale with respect to spatial organization and the relationships between the rooms and salons.

31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.name: Statue of Cardinal Lavigerie
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.author: Bechir Yazidi
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.keywords: French protectorate of Tunisia; missionaries in Tunisia
31671ff1-195a-54da-8c1f-6f9b776bf0e8.description2: On the 23 November 1925, the French resident-general in Tunisia, Lucien Saint, organised a solemn gathering to commemorate 100 years since Cardinal Lavigerie's birth. The municipality of Tunis also received a statue of him brandishing a cross by the sculptor Élie-Jean Vézien, which they chose to put in Place Bab el-Bhar (at the entrance to the medina), a place of great importance to Tunisians. This choice of location angered the Tunisian population and triggered a protest from the students of the Zaytuna University, who considered this act an attack on their religious beliefs (it was placed close to the Zaytuna Mosque) and their traditions. The statue stayed there until Tunisian independence, when it was removed by the Mayor of Tunis.  Lavigerie was the Archbishop of Algiers and Carthage, and the founder of the Pères Blancs in 1868.

32e505cb-9f9d-5883-b87d-e0aff2e6436e.name: Pera Palace Hotel
32e505cb-9f9d-5883-b87d-e0aff2e6436e.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
32e505cb-9f9d-5883-b87d-e0aff2e6436e.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; Ancient İstanbul; hotel; travelling
32e505cb-9f9d-5883-b87d-e0aff2e6436e.description2: Pera Palace Hotel was built in 1892 for the purpose of hosting the passengers of the Orient Express and was named after its location. Alexander Vallaury, a French-Turkish architect living in the city designed the hotel in a blend of neo-classical, art nouveau and oriental styles. The hotel was the first building in Turkey to be powered by electricity other than the Ottoman Palaces. It was also the only address in the city to provide hot running water for its guests and was home to the first electric elevator in Istanbul.

3322889b-90a0-56de-acf0-715553f9bb35.name: Map of Beirut as it appeared in 1841

3322889b-90a0-56de-acf0-715553f9bb35.keywords: Beirut; Mediterranean; Ancient harbour; Coastal geomorphology; Port; Coastline
3322889b-90a0-56de-acf0-715553f9bb35.description2: This map shows Beirut before construction works were taken to modernise the harbour. The coastline has changed significantly since then.

348adef4-1494-549d-bfba-21cff66740ba.description2: A 19th photography focus  the hall of a bourgeois residence: at Barahona's Palace, in a rural city: Évora. This photo shows the bourgeois inside domestic glamour, with some influences of the luxury oriental palaces.

34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.name: *Portico of the Temple at Edfu, Upper Egypt*
34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.description2: Considered the best preserved cult temple of ancient Egypt, Edfu temple was swamped with sand in Roberts’s days, and houses had been built on top. The French archaeologist Auguste Mariette eventually excavated it in the 1860s.This view shows the temple's portico, its  sand-filled façade supported by six monumental columns. The columns on either side of the centre have large lotus columns, those flanking them are made to resemble vertically rising date palm fronds. The outermost columns carry capitals derived from composite Theban palm tree designs. Beyond the columns of the facade, two further rows of capitaled columns form the inner area of the portico, or pronaos. Over the entrance of the portico and on the upper shafts of the columns, pharaonic imagery, emblems, cartouches and hieroglyphs are clearly visible.  The artist emphasizes the monumentality of both the portico and the masses of sand that have invaded it by introducing a group of dwarfed visitors resting on one of the sand dunes in the centre – utterly dwarfed by their surroundings.

34ebe371-2a09-50f9-8e86-921fabe509cc.artist_deathplace: David Roberts: London; Louis Hague: London

351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.name: Au Palais Arabe. A furniture shop of the Italians Eugenio and Alfredo Coen in Tunis
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.dates: Photograph: first years of the 20th century; building: late 19th–early 20th century
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.author: Giulia Barrera
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.archival: Comitato della Camera italiana di commercio ed arti, *Gli italiani in Tunisia*, Tunis, 1906, p. 164
351e4901-7c17-581f-9b15-8be1d6fc3458.description2: “Au Palais Arabe”, Rue de Rome, 3, Tunis, was once the most important shop in town for furniture and other household items. Eugenio Coen (born in Livorno in 1855, migrated to Tunis in 1885) and his brother Alfredo (born in Livorno in 1868 and migrated to Tunis in 1887) also ran a furniture factory that, in 1906, employed about 100 carpenters, cabinet makers and other workers, 80 per cent of whom were Italian.

351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.name: *Mosque of Sidi Bu Madyan, Tlemcen, Algeria*
351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
351f1d5e-9300-5133-9200-12abc5718e8c.description2: The mosque adjoins the shrine of Sidi Bu Madyan, a twelfth century holy-man, and was built by the Marinid dynasty in 1339. Fabrizi's view shows clearly the richly carved stucco decoration framing the simple horseshoe arches; through one of these is seen the tiled mihrab (niche indicating the direction of Mecca) and the wooden minbar (pulpit). Fabrizi has captured the moment after the formal prayers when each worshipper makes a personal supplication to Allah, holding his hands out in a gesture to receive His blessing.

357f3042-331f-5bd6-8477-6430aa4c18a4.name: Ouled el-Hamra Mosque
357f3042-331f-5bd6-8477-6430aa4c18a4.history: Construction began at the end of the 18th century, but the mosque was not completed until the 19th century. It underwent several stages of expansion, especially during the reign of Sultan al-Hasan I, when similar mosques were constructed in Tangier and Asilah.
357f3042-331f-5bd6-8477-6430aa4c18a4.keywords: Religious building; Islamic art; Islamic architecture; Islamic architecture in Morocco; Islamic influence; traditional building; traditional city; city; urban space; Islamic city; Islamic urban space; plan; Moroccan city; urban planning; maghribi minaret; zellij; ceramic; applied arts; geometrical decoration; geometrical motifs; public space
357f3042-331f-5bd6-8477-6430aa4c18a4.description2: Occupying a space relative to its size, the mosque covers an area of 1,200m². Its square-shaped minaret is similar to those seen throughout the Muslim West, divided into five sections of sandstone decorated with green *zellige*. The *zellige* decoration is continued on the facade of the mosque, forming a lobed valance or *lambrequin*. Small rectangular openings are apparently recent additions, as are the green tiles on the pitched roof. There is a single fountain for ablutions.

3834322c-3b30-5333-9de0-37e6dc5efe5d.name: The statue of Hadrian
3834322c-3b30-5333-9de0-37e6dc5efe5d.dates: The Tiled Kiosk: 15th century; the photograph: 19th century; emperor Hadrian: 76—138 A.D.
3834322c-3b30-5333-9de0-37e6dc5efe5d.description2: Hadrian was the fourteenth Emperor of Rome (10 August 117 to 10 July 138 CE) and is known as the third of the Five Good Emperors (Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and Marcus Aurelius) who ruled justly. The statue of the famous Roman Emperor Hadrian is located in the Roman hall of the museum. Hadrian was depicted with a figure under his foot. The statue was found in Crete.

3940c19d-aee8-57e8-88f6-9ecbdf782174.name: Ancient Egyptian Agricultural museum display hall
3940c19d-aee8-57e8-88f6-9ecbdf782174.author: Ibrahim Abdel Aziz
3940c19d-aee8-57e8-88f6-9ecbdf782174.history:
King Fu\`ad I chose the palace of Fatma Ismail, the daughter of Khedive Ismail, ‎to host the displays of the Agricultural Museum. The ‎palace was chosen due to its location near the Egyptian Ministry of Agriculture in the ‎neighborhood of Dokki in Cairo.  
The museum, which was first called "The Agricultural Museum of King Fu\`ad I", was officially opened for the public on the 16th of January 1938 in a big ceremony that the king himself attended.
3940c19d-aee8-57e8-88f6-9ecbdf782174.keywords: Agricultural museum; Dokki, Agriculture Palace; Khedive Ismail; King Fu`ad I; Princess Fatma; Khedivial palaces; Khedivial Egypt; Ancient Agriculture; Pharaonic Agriculture
3940c19d-aee8-57e8-88f6-9ecbdf782174.description2: The museum of Ancient Egyptian Agriculture is the most interesting section of the Agricultural Museum and it contains the most valuable displays. Tourist groups must receive permission beforehand in order to visit this museum. It represents the first section of the development of agriculture in Egypt ‎and it illustrates the ‎history of Egyptian agriculture from the prehistoric period till the late Pharaonic ‎period. ‎The first floor of the museum of Ancient Egyptian Agriculture hosts all sorts of ‎displays that illustrate how the ancient Egyptians cultivated their lands. The displays ‎include ancient tools and equipment that were used in the days of the Pharaohs and descriptions of ‎how the ancient Egyptians created these tools.

39c4d9ff-e32f-5e06-bea2-e9873ae36a23.name: National Evangelical Church of Beirut
39c4d9ff-e32f-5e06-bea2-e9873ae36a23.description: The National Evangelical Church of Beirut is the first native Arabic Protestant congregation in the Middle East. It acts as the headquarters and administrative centre for the nine evangelical churches which operate under the name of the National Evangelical Union of Lebanon. Today, the church organises social, cultural, and educational activities, and runs two schools in Beirut and one in the Beqaa. It is also involved with the theological education at the Near East School of Theology in Beirut.
39c4d9ff-e32f-5e06-bea2-e9873ae36a23.author: Julien El Khoury, Jeff El-Msanne
39c4d9ff-e32f-5e06-bea2-e9873ae36a23.history: Established in 1848 by Congregational and Presbyterian American missionaries, the National Evangelical Church of Beirut is the oldest and largest of nine congregations situated inside Beirut. The church acted as a centre for the activities and celebrations for both the English and Arabic speaking communities until it was completely destroyed during the Lebanese Civil war. The clock tower was the only aspect of the church to survive the war, and the church itself was rebuilt in 1998. Today, it is fully functioning and located in Beirut's Central District.
39c4d9ff-e32f-5e06-bea2-e9873ae36a23.keywords: church; Evangelical; tourism; site; monument; religion; Protestant

3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.name: The Ottoman Bank
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph bank; economy
3ae243ba-330f-5d5a-a7ac-1134d23470a9.description2: One of the world's largest photo archives, Abdülhamid II's photo archives – knows as the Yildiz Albums – contain about 37 thousand pictures from that period of the Ottoman Empire. The photo archives contain images of cities, buildings which were built by sultan, schools, students, soldiers, mosques, ports, government departments, shipyards, railways, bridges, bazaars, machines, locomotives and factories. The Ottoman Bank was founded in 1856 in the Galata business section of Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire, as a joint venture between British interests, the Banque de Paris et des Pays-Bas of France, and the Ottoman government. *Tanzimat* era's principal renovations in the financial field were the reestablishment of the currency and the foundation of the Ottoman Bank.

3d0e6f9c-00ca-5d85-9d59-e3d8520d4abc.name: Saint Georges Maronite Cathedral
3d0e6f9c-00ca-5d85-9d59-e3d8520d4abc.description: Designed by the Italian architect Giuseppe Maggiore in the neo-classical style, the Saint George Cathedral bears great resemblance to the Basilica di Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome.
