7a05190e-1927-5037-ba2d-10e15038ab09.description2: Dar al-Makina consists of three distinct areas with several partition walls, but also some extensions and doors for communication with the outside. In fact, the interior of the main building is dominated by a forest of pillars, which together form a square section that connects with the upper level of horseshoe arches and stilted and round arches. Building materials used for the elevation of these elements consist primarily of traditional solid brick, built according to the ancient technique known in Fez, with mortar of lime and sand, and rarely, in some of the load-bearing walls, with stone fragments. The entirety is covered internally with a smooth coating of lime and sand which is whitewashed.

7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.name: Record of the marriage between the Egyptian governmental official Paul Draneht Bey, aged 55, and the Italian Adele Casati, aged 19, celebrated in Oggebbio (Italy) in 1873
7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.author: Massimiliano Cremona, Ignazio Galella
7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.archival: AS VB, Comune di Oggebbio, Registro Atti di Matrimonio, vol. 523/24, firme degli sposi
7a673124-7bea-543e-8cdf-59c06cdc2216.description2: Apparently, Adelaide Casati and her sister Margarita attended the premiere of the Aida in Cairo (24 December 1871). Their father, Filippo, was participating in the performance as a cello player. In Cairo, the two Casati sisters met their future husbands, respectively, Paul Draneht, and the Greek banker, Joannis Sinadino (who acted as witness in the marriage between Paul Draneht and Adelaide Casati). Both men moved to live in Oggebbio, Italy, when Paul Draneht bought a villa there.

7a6f5cad-f74c-5502-95b2-2068560418a6.name: The Port From The Galata Tower
7a6f5cad-f74c-5502-95b2-2068560418a6.keywords: Photograph; Old İstanbul Photograph; İstanbul; Abdullah Brothers
7a6f5cad-f74c-5502-95b2-2068560418a6.description2: Abdullah Brothers is the name given to three men of Armenian origin, Viçen (1820-1902), Hovsep Abdullahyan (1830-1908) and Kevork (1839-1918) who started the art of photography in Turkey. For 40 years they photographed the people of Istanbul, landscapes, various political and social events, and prepared albums of historical and cultural values, as well as monuments.

7aaccebe-2608-5891-9e82-c06d9f7a2f1f.name: Traditional house
7aaccebe-2608-5891-9e82-c06d9f7a2f1f.description: Houses in the 19th century were modestly built; the roof was generally supported by wooden beams, and stone stairs were built inside the house to access the upper floors (although many other houses only had wooden stairs).
7aaccebe-2608-5891-9e82-c06d9f7a2f1f.history: The houses were built with wooden windows which were filled with tinted glass. A balcony could usually be found on the first floor, which was covered with a clear window for lighting and ventilation purposes. This architectural style was clearly influenced by European architecture and design, indicating the growing influence of European culture and trends in 19th century Beirut and elsewhere in the region.

7b607aac-e5db-517f-aaf5-04ce4eb5e62c.name: *Project for a Garden or Park*
7b607aac-e5db-517f-aaf5-04ce4eb5e62c.author: Ana Cabrera
7b607aac-e5db-517f-aaf5-04ce4eb5e62c.artist: Architect: J. Croentdtelo y Victoriano Durán
7b607aac-e5db-517f-aaf5-04ce4eb5e62c.keywords: Architecture design; Parks; Urban facilities; Neo-mudejar style
7b607aac-e5db-517f-aaf5-04ce4eb5e62c.description2: This project for a park with fountain, covered, possibly, with tiles decorated in Neo-Mudéjar style. The development of urban design was an important subject from the mid-19th century onwards. The Neo-Mudéjar style was selected by the architects for important buildings such as theatres or bull rings or urban spaces as the International exhibition of Barcelona 1888. One of the characteristics of this style is use of brick and tile decoration in the buildings’ interiors and façades.

7e3011a6-9b62-55da-a642-e474bf775d1f.name: Bosporus, Istanbul
7e3011a6-9b62-55da-a642-e474bf775d1f.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
7e3011a6-9b62-55da-a642-e474bf775d1f.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; Ancient Istanbul
7e3011a6-9b62-55da-a642-e474bf775d1f.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century.

7e932bea-47e5-5386-9498-0e48388f3e95.name: Fountain
7e932bea-47e5-5386-9498-0e48388f3e95.author: Marie Therese Moujabber
7e932bea-47e5-5386-9498-0e48388f3e95.description2: Water fountains such as these were common in Ottoman government buildings in Lebanon, and were turned on whenever there was a meeting to prevent outsiders overhearing or eavesdropping. This marble fountain is octagonal in shape and is decorated with embossed semi-cylinders on each side. The exterior of the structure is decorated with a mosaic of black, white, beige and brown marble organised in geometric designs. A second, circular level of the fountain rests on this first octagonal structure.

8138d27f-0df1-5e19-884f-c3f2fabf66df.name: Istanbul Main Post Office Opening Ceremony
8138d27f-0df1-5e19-884f-c3f2fabf66df.artist: Photograph: author unknown; building: architect Vedat Tek, architect Muzaffer Bey
8138d27f-0df1-5e19-884f-c3f2fabf66df.keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service; communication
8138d27f-0df1-5e19-884f-c3f2fabf66df.description2: The Istanbul Main Post Office is an office building for postal services located at the *Sirkeci* quarter of the faith district in Istanbul, Turkey. It was designed by architect Vedat Tek in the First Turkish National architectural style and was constructed between 1903 and 1909. (Vedat Tek was a notable Turkish architect, who has been one of the leading figures of the First Turkish National Architectural Movement. He studied at the *École Centrale Paris*, graduating with a degree in civil engineering before he got his further education in architecture at the *Ecole des Beaux Arts* in Paris.) The four-story building houses a post office, the *Sirkeci* Post Office, office space for regional administration and also since 2000 the Istanbul Postal Museum. It is Turkey's largest post office building.

81a863b7-0e26-5e2a-b1ac-55b331836571.name: The Consuls’ Square [Alexandria, Egypt] after the Fire
81a863b7-0e26-5e2a-b1ac-55b331836571.author: Giulia Barrera
81a863b7-0e26-5e2a-b1ac-55b331836571.second_name: The ruins of the Consuls' Square in Alexandria (Egypt) after the bombing of the city by the British Navy in 1882
81a863b7-0e26-5e2a-b1ac-55b331836571.description2:
The author of this picture, Luigi Fiorillo, was an Italian photographer who migrated to Alexandria (Egypt) around 1870 and opened a successful photography shop. In 1877, he participated as photographer in an expedition to Shewa region (Ethiopia), organised by the Italian Geographical Society, and ten years later in an Italian military expedition for the colonial conquest of Eritrea.  
In 1882, Fiorillo was one of the few Europeans who remained in Alexandria after the anti-foreign rioting and documented the consequences of the British bombardment on Alexandria of July 11th. He collected 50 pictures of the city ruins in an album titled “Souvenir d'Alexandrie: Ruines, 1882”.  
On the back of some photos that he took in the 1880s, Fiorillo defines himself as “le photographe de Son Altesse le Prince Mohammed Toussoun Pasha” (the photographer of his Majesty Prince Mohammed Toussoun Pasha). Luigi Fiorillo died in 1898.

en: Silingardi, Adriano, ”Luigi Fiorillo, l’avventuroso fotografo di Alessandria d’Egitto”, unpublished paper (available on line) for the exhibition of the same name, Genoa, 2014.

82418ca9-7d43-5ee2-913a-f1235ecfd9e4.name: House
82418ca9-7d43-5ee2-913a-f1235ecfd9e4.author: Nada Andonovska (author), Prof. Petar Namichev (consultant)
82418ca9-7d43-5ee2-913a-f1235ecfd9e4.history: The most intense development of urban houses in Macedonia occurred in the 19th century, creating a new panorama of towns across the landscape. This applies particularly to the town of Veles, which reached the peak of its rise in the mid-19th century, owing to extensive growth of crafts and trade.
82418ca9-7d43-5ee2-913a-f1235ecfd9e4.description2: In this house the influence of the Levantine architecture was coupled with the individual skills and talents of native architects, which has given rise to a diversity of types and outstanding autochthonous construction solutions. This three-storied house was built by use of the bondruk structural system, which consists of wooden framing and adobe. The façade is coated with mortar and decorated by application of a strip pattern on the band between the second and third storey, as well as above the top storey. It also has painted ornaments applied on the surface under the roof.

83126725-c2b3-5d22-9ee2-4e1c45c60872.name: Patriarchal Monument
83126725-c2b3-5d22-9ee2-4e1c45c60872.description: This building has been the main headquarters of the Maronite Patriarchate since 1790.
83126725-c2b3-5d22-9ee2-4e1c45c60872.author: Jeff El-Msanne
83126725-c2b3-5d22-9ee2-4e1c45c60872.history: Patriarch John Hajj, who renovated this monastery, was elected in 1890 following the death of Patriarch Mas'ad. He expanded the structure by adding a second floor.

84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.name: *Entrance to Damascus*
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.artist: W. H. McFarlane (after a drawing by Harry Fenn 1838 – 1911)
84d5ec45-7bab-5d25-96f2-a48ed1fe7a85.description2: This coloured engraving by W. H. McFarlane shows the entrance to Damascus by the new French-built road through the Merj, or meadow, west of the city. Most probably this is the carriage road that had been established between Beirut and Damascus in 1863, at a time when most other connecting arterties were mere mule paths. French firms also built railways and ports in Syria during the later 19th century. The Ottoman style building in the background on the right is the Tekkiye Mosque Complex, built on the banks of the Barada river at the orders of Suleiman the Magnificent between 1554-1560 and incorporating a mosque, accomodation, a soup kitchen and a hospice.

8653fc72-b87d-51ed-9732-e87d6b42578c.name: The Palace of the Poste Italienne (Ruins)
8653fc72-b87d-51ed-9732-e87d6b42578c.author: Giulia Barrera
8653fc72-b87d-51ed-9732-e87d6b42578c.second_name: The ruins of the Italian Post Office in Alexandria (Egypt) after the bombing of the city by the British Navy in 1882
8653fc72-b87d-51ed-9732-e87d6b42578c.description2:
The author of this picture, Luigi Fiorillo, was an Italian photographer who migrated to Alexandria (Egypt) around 1870 and opened a successful photography shop. In 1877, he participated as photographer in an expedition to Shewa region (Ethiopia), organised by the Italian Geographical Society, and ten years later in an Italian military expedition for the colonial conquest of Eritrea.  
In 1882, Fiorillo was one of the few Europeans who remained in Alexandria after the anti-foreign rioting and documented the consequences of the British bombardment on Alexandria of July 11th. He collected 50 pictures of the city ruins in an album titled “Souvenir d'Alexandrie: Ruines, 1882”.  
On the back of some photos that he took in the 1880s Fiorillo defines himself as “le photographe de Son Altesse le Prince Mohammed Toussoun Pasha” (the photographer of his Majesty Prince Mohammed Toussoun Pasha). Luigi Fiorillo died in 1898.

875b22bd-4eaf-5621-a282-05cb962a752c.name: Sursuq Palace
875b22bd-4eaf-5621-a282-05cb962a752c.description: Other than some nineteenth century plaster-work in the reception rooms which resembles Sicilian palaces of the time, and the employment of some Italian craftsmen, the Sursuq House was built in a strictly traditional Lebanese architectural and aesthetic style. This is indicated first and foremost by the use of a single large block. The Great Hall consists of four sets of traditional Lebanese triple-arches, each supported by fluted marble pillars. The house’s painted furnishings were commissioned and designed privately. It also contains a series of glass cabinets, displaying various valuable collections, including second century glassware and Lebanese jewellery. The garden is one of the largest gardens left in the city, with many landowners having sold their properties to speculative building projects. The kiosk in the garden, which was converted into a Turkish baths when the house was built in 1860, predates the main house and is used as visitor rooms today.
875b22bd-4eaf-5621-a282-05cb962a752c.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
875b22bd-4eaf-5621-a282-05cb962a752c.history: Built in 1860 for Musa Sursuq, in Rue Sursuq, Sursuq Palace is now the residence of his grand-daughter Lady Yvonne Cochrane, who inherited the estate at the age of two. Of all the Sursuq houses, this is the largest and the only one that preserves its original splendour. Its second owner, Lady Cochrane's father Alfred Bey Sursuq, increased the size of the gardens and expanded the house's collection of valuable pictures, carpets and objets d'art.

87af700d-97ab-50c7-9235-e6cd264dbbcc.name: Plaque on the rocks of Nahr al-Kalb documenting the end of WWI
87af700d-97ab-50c7-9235-e6cd264dbbcc.holder: Nahr al-Kalb Authority, Ministry of Tourism
87af700d-97ab-50c7-9235-e6cd264dbbcc.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
87af700d-97ab-50c7-9235-e6cd264dbbcc.keywords: Politics; Army; World War I; Battalion; Memory
87af700d-97ab-50c7-9235-e6cd264dbbcc.description2: This plaque was erected by the French General Gouraud in 1920 to commemorate the entry of French troops in Damascus and their subsequent victory at the battle of Maysalun in July 1920. The text, written in French, is composed of 22 lines and lists the names of the battalions that took part in the battle. The plaque is decorated with bronze embellishments.

87f34acd-b200-5f1a-b478-34b80e307ce2.name: Spanish Franciscan Church of Buenaventura
87f34acd-b200-5f1a-b478-34b80e307ce2.history: Built in 1890, the church closed in 1968 and remained abandoned until fairly recently. When restoration of the Old *Medina* began, the church was selected for renovation and now has exhibition and media spaces, a comprehensive library of over 6,000 titles and a discovery space for children.
87f34acd-b200-5f1a-b478-34b80e307ce2.keywords: Religious building; Islamic art; Islamic architecture; Islamic architecture in Morocco; Islamic influence; traditional building; traditional city; city; urban space; Islamic city; Islamic urban space; plan; urban planning; church; Spanish in Morocco; Moroccan city; Christians in Morocco; migration; work
87f34acd-b200-5f1a-b478-34b80e307ce2.description2: Built for the Spanish community based in Casablanca, this church stands in the Old *Medina* on land donated by Sultan Mulay al-Hasan I. The construction of this church testifies to the improving relationship between Morocco and Spain and highlights the importance of the Spanish community in Casablanca, which was very active in the port sector and played a dynamic role in the local and international economy.

88655ec5-19eb-505b-a6c2-72dc2d1fac7d.name: The Cotton Museum at the Agricultural museum
88655ec5-19eb-505b-a6c2-72dc2d1fac7d.author: Ibrahim Abdel Aziz
88655ec5-19eb-505b-a6c2-72dc2d1fac7d.history:
King Fu\`ad I chose the palace of Fatma Ismail, the daughter of Khedive Ismail, ‎to host the displays of the Agricultural Museum. The ‎palace was chosen due to its location near the Egyptian Ministry of Agriculture in the ‎neighborhood of Dokki in Cairo. ‎  
The museum, which was first called "The Agricultural Museum of King Fu\`ad I", was officially opened for the public on the 16th of January 1938 in a big ceremony that the king himself attended.
88655ec5-19eb-505b-a6c2-72dc2d1fac7d.description2: This building is used as a display museum to show the types of cotton seeds and strains in Egypt next to the products that come from each type. Egyptian cotton is preferred around the world because of its long fibre, which make it softer and stronger at the same time. For many years, it was so valuable that most of the crop was exported to European countries, and Egyptians themselves could hardly buy items made from its cloth.

898f2296-ee1f-5e48-a6ee-73f0b9a210a9.name: *Head of the Great Sphinx, Pyramids of Geezeh July 17th, 1839*
898f2296-ee1f-5e48-a6ee-73f0b9a210a9.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Authority
898f2296-ee1f-5e48-a6ee-73f0b9a210a9.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
898f2296-ee1f-5e48-a6ee-73f0b9a210a9.description2: Roberts depicted the Sphinx some twenty years after Giovanni Battista Caviglia had excavated at Giza in 1817 and had cleared masses of sand away from the monument, which up to that point had been buried right up to its neck. Subsequently, he succeeded in clearing the whole front of the Sphinx. At the point of Roberts’ visit, the sphinx was visible from the top of the head to the floor of the temple between its paws. After its initial discovery, the Sphinx soon became one of the foremost fascinations for early European Egyptologists, including Auguste Mariette, the founder and first director of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, Gaston Maspero, who conducted a survey  of it in 1886, and the British scholar E. A. Wallis Budge.It also proved fascinating for Orientalist artists and artisans all over Europe. In Roberts' artwork, the stone-cut monument is rendered in great detail, carefully recording also the far-reaching damage to the Sphinx’s face, the cause of which had already given rise to much discussion and speculation at the time. The Pyramids in this view are that of Cheops, or the Great Pyramid, seen on the right, and on the left, that of Cephren, also known as the Second Pyramid.
898f2296-ee1f-5e48-a6ee-73f0b9a210a9.artist_birthplace: David Roberts: Edinburgh, Scotland; Louis Hague: Tournai, Belgium
898f2296-ee1f-5e48-a6ee-73f0b9a210a9.artist_deathplace: David Roberts: London; Louis Hague: London

8b3e69ba-c1ec-5cc8-a491-c79fd70669f0.name: Imaret
8b3e69ba-c1ec-5cc8-a491-c79fd70669f0.holder: IMARET – Institute Mohammed Ali for the Research of the Eastern Tradition (under contract with the Egyptian Waqf Organization)
8b3e69ba-c1ec-5cc8-a491-c79fd70669f0.author: I.M.A.R.E.T.
8b3e69ba-c1ec-5cc8-a491-c79fd70669f0.history: With the passage of time, the charitable and educational purposes of the foundation declined. According to surviving records, the School continued to function as late as 1902, and the Soup Kitchen as late as 1923. After the Lausanne Treaty and the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey, the complex housed Greek refugees from Asia Minor (1927–1960). In 1954, Imaret was listed as a protected historical monument by the Greek Government. A series of (never realized) agreements between Greece and Egypt to restore the monument followed. In August 2001, a contract was signed between the Egyptian Waqf Organization and the Missirian family, who undertook the demanding task of restoring the two monuments and attributing them to new uses.
8b3e69ba-c1ec-5cc8-a491-c79fd70669f0.keywords: 19th century Ottoman baroque; Waqf; educational and charitable foundation; Mohammed Ali; Egypt; secular education in the Ottoman Empire
8b3e69ba-c1ec-5cc8-a491-c79fd70669f0.description2: *Imaret* was an educational and charitable foundation, donated by Mohammed ‘Ali, founder of modern Egypt, to his hometown. The complex included an elementary school and two higher level colleges dedicated to the instruction of the traditional Islamic curriculum, modern sciences and mathematics. It is one of the earliest examples of western style technical school providing secular education in the Ottoman Empire and reflects Mohammed ‘Ali’s program of modernization. The complex had 61 rooms for up to 300 boarding students, two study halls, a library, a printing press and a soup kitchen to feed students, travellers and the poor, regardless of religion. To meet the religious and hygiene needs of its occupants, the complex also contained a place for prayer, fountains for ablutions and a hammam. Cisterns underneath the structure guaranteed a continuous source of water.

8baf4fe2-defb-5e01-a35e-a1897a77d6e1.name: *Typical North African house in the Sahel*
8baf4fe2-defb-5e01-a35e-a1897a77d6e1.author: Dalila Orfali
8baf4fe2-defb-5e01-a35e-a1897a77d6e1.keywords: Painting; North Africa; Algeria; city; house
8baf4fe2-defb-5e01-a35e-a1897a77d6e1.description2: Ottoman-era architecture was a popular theme among European artists of the 18th and 19th centuries.

8be256e6-ef08-535a-9646-fcfbd6751a6c.name: Beylerbeyi Palace
8be256e6-ef08-535a-9646-fcfbd6751a6c.keywords: Seaside palace; pavilion; Ottoman architecture; Bosphorus Strait; Sultan Abdülaziz
8be256e6-ef08-535a-9646-fcfbd6751a6c.description2: One of the most magnificent Ottoman coastal palaces, Beylerbeyi Palace is located on the Asian coast of the Bosphorus. It was commissioned by Sultan Abdülaziz and consists of the main palace structure and its auxiliaries. Its façade and interior decorations blend various Western influences with Eastern motifs. This summer residence is remarkable for its rich decoration and its two sea-pavilions on the water are the most striking and typical examples of Orientalism in Istanbul. It was opened to the public as a museum in 1984.

8d2e560e-b2b4-59b4-9f4e-b644abc31a4b.name: *The England Hotel*
8d2e560e-b2b4-59b4-9f4e-b644abc31a4b.keywords: Hotel; Landmarks of Egypt; Old Hotels; Tourism
8d2e560e-b2b4-59b4-9f4e-b644abc31a4b.description2: The England Hotel is one of the historical hotels built during the British occupation of Egypt.

8dec350b-560d-5475-8a47-00b9dd25268c.name: Medal of Emperor Franz Joseph I
8dec350b-560d-5475-8a47-00b9dd25268c.keywords: Emperor Franz Joseph; Suez; Suez Canal; Egypt; numismatics
8dec350b-560d-5475-8a47-00b9dd25268c.description2: A medal depicting the symbolic figure of Egypt sitting on a sphinx. In the background, the three pyramids of Giza and a sailing ship can be seen. The opposite side of the medal has a portrait of Emperor Franz Joseph. The medal was created in commemoration of the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869.

8e50c089-18d5-5800-bdb6-e0c14282ea69.name: St Justa's lift
8e50c089-18d5-5800-bdb6-e0c14282ea69.author: Cristina Correia
8e50c089-18d5-5800-bdb6-e0c14282ea69.history: Built between 1890–1892 it will be inaugurated still unfinished by Royal Prince Afonso of Braganza (1865–1920) on the 18th August 1892.
8e50c089-18d5-5800-bdb6-e0c14282ea69.keywords: Lisbon; Urban innovation; transportation; Urban iron architecture
8e50c089-18d5-5800-bdb6-e0c14282ea69.architects: Engineer Raul Mesnier du Ponsard (1849–1914 Porto/Inhambane); master builder and Foreman of the building sites: Manuel Cardoso (n.d.)
8e50c089-18d5-5800-bdb6-e0c14282ea69.description2:
This revivalist example of the 1900 iron architecture for transportation foregrounds amidst Lisbon Downtown skyline. The 45 m high lift includes a gangway with Neo-gothic decoration 2 towers with 7 floors, each one with a cabin for 24 passengers. Inside they are covered with wood and mirrors while each floor has its own decoration. The balance between the cabins is provided by a steel cable and was initially water moved.  
Foreseen since 1874 it aimed to overcome the 25 metres gap between Ouro and Carmo Streets thus easing the pedestrian’ traffic between the hills of the Lisbon centre. The inauguration of the gangway by King Carlos I was held in 1901 and the lift itself started to be fully operational in 1902 and electrified in 1907.  
It is classified as a national monument.

8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.name: *Nosocomium* \[Latin: Hospital\]
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.author: Marina Minozzi
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.keywords: Italian painters; city; urban space; segregation; medicine; disease; poverty; illness; life expectancy; psychiatry; social changes; scientific development; social topics; post-unitarian Italian society; Positivism; celebration of science; exposition
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.copyright: Copyright image: Soprintendenza alla Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea.
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.description2: Silvio Rotta was introduced to painting by his father and, in his early years, produced mainly watercolours, genre compositions inspired by Venetian popular customs. In 1887, after an illness, the production of the artist underwent a radical change ad began to show social realism through the depiction of the insane. *Nosocomium* represents a psychiatric hospital where poor and sick were hosted and nursed. The scale of the canvas is accentuated by the diagonal of the benches and the path. The painting won awards at the 1895 Biennale of Venice and is now recognised as one of the most important works by Rotta. The scene’s realism offers a merciless analysis and public complaint about the patients’ living conditions. Caring of poor and sick was an important issue during the 19th century and a law to control hospitals and mental institution was discussed in those years.
8efde259-472d-50ce-9578-75e8ff556e35.holding_institution_org: Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea (GNAM)

en: Picciau, M., in Elena di Majo and Mateo Lafranconi (eds), *Galleria Nazionale d’Arte Moderna. Le Collezioni. Il XIX secolo*, Milan: Electa, 2006, cat. 11.16.

8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.name: Beirut Port before expansion
8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury, Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.keywords: Commerce; Expansion; Economy; Trading; Goods; Transportation; Port; Harbor; Communication; Beirut
8f60990a-2e19-50e5-b91c-31a7c8a103fd.description2: This photograph shows the Beirut port before its expansion. The dam was built under the command of Ibrahim Pasha. This old port underwent several important changes in the late 19th century, including the construction of a commercial tribunal and expansion of the port. This expansion involved the enlargement of existing buildings and filling areas of sea with rock brought in along the Nahr al-Kalb railway.

8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.name: *Panoramic View of Makkah - Arabia (West Asia). Panoramic View of Makkah during the Celebration of the Pilgrimage of the Muslims to the Kaaba, where the religious treasure is guarded*
8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation / Sharjah Museums Authority
8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.dimensions: 330 mm x 240 mm (image only, without margin)
8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.third_name: *Vista Panoramica de la Meca - Arabia (Asia Occidental). Vista Panoramica de la Meca Al Celebrarse una Peregrinacion de los Mahometos á la Kaaba Donde se custodia el tesoro religioso*
8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.description2: This coloured print, perhaps from a late 19th-century, Spanish newspaper or magazine, shows a birds-eye view of the city of Makkah with the Holy Mosque and Ka'bah at the centre. The view was recorded from one of the rugged mountains surrounding the city. Hundreds of pilgrims are seen to approach from afar and converge on the city gates. that lead to the sanctuary. The print shows close compositional similarities to an early 19th century drawing by the English officer and artist Charles Hamilton Smith (1776-1859). Smith, although not known to have visited the Arabian peninsula, produced an album of drawings - possibly in turn taken from older engravings - with views from Syria, Persia and Arabia sometime between 1818 and 1846.

9061ae44-6d42-5964-b1e3-97aaad10a6fc.name: Arènes de Lutèce
9061ae44-6d42-5964-b1e3-97aaad10a6fc.description2: The "Arènes de Lutèce" (a Gallo-Roman amphitheatre) was rediscovered during various urbanisation projects between 1869 and 1885. It was registered as a historical monument thanks to the intervention of the Société des Amis des Arènes and Victor Hugo.

90fa424c-bb73-5fd9-ae3d-bc20de07992b.name: Yıldız Palace The World-Displayer Kiosk (Cihannuma Kiosk)
90fa424c-bb73-5fd9-ae3d-bc20de07992b.notice: This is an unedited Database entry and may contain errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are working to raise the funds required to complete the editing; should you wish to contribute please visit our [Support page](https://www.museumwnf.org/atrium_support.php).
90fa424c-bb73-5fd9-ae3d-bc20de07992b.history:
Yildiz Palace, which is the last architectural example of Turkish Ottoman palace, is located on the Yildiz hill in the district of Besiktas. Sultan Ahmed I was the first to build a pavilion, over this land registered at the time to the Private treasury of the Ottoman Sultan as a hunting place sultans beginning during the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566).  
The main construction in the palace started in the period of Sultan Abdulhamid II (1876-1909) and it was called Saray-i Humayun (Central palace). During this period the palace comprised of buildings for private use of the sultan as well as buildings, allocated for the officials, repair shops and carpentry like repairing shop, carpenter’s shop and the buildings of culture and art such as theatre, museum and library. The Palace begun to serve as a museum under the name of “Directorate of the Museum of Yildiz Palace since 1993.
90fa424c-bb73-5fd9-ae3d-bc20de07992b.description2: The Kiosk, named *Cihannüma* (“World-displayer”) for its wide vision field including Bosphorus, the Golden Horn and Marmara Sea, was built on Hasbahçe as a kiosk for resting and watching. It is one of the most remarkable buildings of the Palace regarding its carpentry work and design elements. Sultan Abdülhamit used the upper story of the Kiosk for watching Istanbul and the Bosphorus with long-sighted binoculars. Because of its panoramic view, it was called as Cihannuma and built as a residence and watching kiosk. This is the most important building of the palace in terms of wooden tectonics and decoration figures. Sultan Abdulhamid II used the upper floor of the kiosk in order to view Istanbul and Bosphorus with effective binoculars.

9113b91c-e517-59d8-b8a9-ea3d96446cd4.name: Salepçioğlu Mosque
9113b91c-e517-59d8-b8a9-ea3d96446cd4.description2: This mosque, built in the Eclectic style with Orientalist elements, illustrates the degree to which the West influenced Anatolia.

918c2c1a-37f3-5178-8124-1d569b29d213.name: Dar Ben Abdallah
918c2c1a-37f3-5178-8124-1d569b29d213.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
918c2c1a-37f3-5178-8124-1d569b29d213.history: This princely palace in the Tunis medina was built in the style of 19th century Italian royal courts, and named after its original owners, who were rich silk weavers. During the French Protectorate era it was brought by a French painter, but was then reacquired by the Tunisian state after independence, at which point it became the Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires of the 19th century Tunisian bourgeoisie.
918c2c1a-37f3-5178-8124-1d569b29d213.description2: The curving hallway, richly decorated with faience pottery, marble and stucco, leads to an open-air courtyard, around which there are several apartments, today housing the museum's collection. The patio is surrounded by porticos with white marble columns. The walls are decorated with Neapolitan faience pottery, above a frieze of carved plaster. At the centre of the patio sits a fountain with three basins made of marble imported from Carrara. On the first floor, a circular gallery with wood railings adds to the palace's opulent style.

9226b1df-56b3-5ffb-a38d-64b0ff5cec56.name: African slaves working the fields
9226b1df-56b3-5ffb-a38d-64b0ff5cec56.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
9226b1df-56b3-5ffb-a38d-64b0ff5cec56.description2: This series of photographs attests to the existence of African slaves working in domestic roles or in agricultural labour.

92edd2fe-ef09-5e83-baba-8f729535104a.name: Dolmabahçe Mosque and Square
92edd2fe-ef09-5e83-baba-8f729535104a.keywords: Photograph; Old İstanbul Photograph; İstanbul; Abdullah Brothers
92edd2fe-ef09-5e83-baba-8f729535104a.description2: Dolmabahçe Mosque’s original construction was initiated by Bezm-i Alem Valide Sultan, the mother of Sultan Abdülmecid (1823-61). Upon her death, its construction was continued by her son. It is located in the southern part of the Dolmabahce Palace, situated on the coast. The mosque was opened for prayer services on 23 March 1855. Its architect is Garabet Balyan, a member of the Balyan family, who built various structures for the Ottoman Empire. The Dolmabahçe Mosque is adorned with various items of both Baroque and Ampir styles, which are reflected in the architectural design of that period. Also, an emergent architectural modernity in the mosque is its circular window design. Such a design had rarely been seen in mosques and civil architecture before this time.

933220c7-ac0f-58a4-bd26-9a2aaf27779a.name: Dar Hussein
933220c7-ac0f-58a4-bd26-9a2aaf27779a.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
933220c7-ac0f-58a4-bd26-9a2aaf27779a.history: Built in the 12th century in the heart of the Banu Khorasan's royal city, this palace was occupied by the nobles of various dynasties who had ruled Ifriqiya. It became the seat of Tunis Municipality in 1858, after being restored and redecorated. The palace is named after the General Hussein, who was president of the municipality’s highest council. From 1882 until independence the palace served as the headquarters for the troops of the French occupation. It then became the seat first of Institut National d’Archéologie et Art, and in 1993 of l'Institut National du Patrimoine.
933220c7-ac0f-58a4-bd26-9a2aaf27779a.keywords: Architecture; Andalusian style; Italian style; stucco; carved wood; painting
933220c7-ac0f-58a4-bd26-9a2aaf27779a.description2: Dar Hussein, one of the most beautiful palaces of the Tunis medina, shows traces of all the different eras of Tunisian architecture, from the Khorasani era through the Andalusian, Turkish and colonial eras.  On the ground floor, four large rooms, including a great hall, surround a peristyle. The neo-corinthian capitals topping the columns were made by Italian sculptors. On the first floor there is an elegant second peristyle in a 19th century Italian style, The galleries are divided up into four apartments, decorated with frescoes painted on faience pottery beneath a frieze of carved plaster.

934b04dc-f3d9-52a1-b4a6-850226ba2bd7.name: The Old German Consulate
934b04dc-f3d9-52a1-b4a6-850226ba2bd7.history: Initially built as a residence, the building was then converted into an administrative office for German consular officials in 1902. In 1919, after the Franco-German Treaty, the building became the property of the *Makhzen*, administered by the Pasha Tazi, and was turned into a school.
934b04dc-f3d9-52a1-b4a6-850226ba2bd7.keywords: German in Morocco; German foreign policy; Moorish style; arch; plaster; stucco; Islamic art; Islamic architecture; Islamic influence; Islamic architecture in Morocco; geometrical motifs
934b04dc-f3d9-52a1-b4a6-850226ba2bd7.description2: This Neo-Moorish style building consists of three floors with three apertures in the form of arches on the first floor, windows of smaller dimensions on the second floor and a narrower top storey, which has two apertures, and whose facade is decorated with ornamental plasterwork. The simplicity of the facade conceals the splendid design of the building’s interior.

93c53f75-811e-5d47-8d12-4f56a360451f.name: Carthage archaeological site
93c53f75-811e-5d47-8d12-4f56a360451f.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
93c53f75-811e-5d47-8d12-4f56a360451f.history: Founded by the Phoenicians around 814 BC, Carthage was the city that brought Africa into mainstream European historical narratives. Hanno's Carthage ruled the seas, and Hannibal's Carthage was master of the land; Carthage certainly saw its golden age before disappearing. Augustus built Carthage as the capital of proconsular Africa, and the Imperial Roman Carthage that succeeded it put great importance on art and literature. Christian Carthage of Saint Augustine's times appeared to be a city fuelled by religion and passion. It was ruled by the Vandals for a century, then the Byzantines and finally the Arabs. However, although the leadership changed many times over the years, Carthage itself did not move. Modern Carthage, therefore, holds the evidence for many different histories. It has been listed as a UNESCO world heritage site since the 26 October 1979.
93c53f75-811e-5d47-8d12-4f56a360451f.keywords: Carthage; Phoenicians; Hannibal; Saint Augustine; Africa
93c53f75-811e-5d47-8d12-4f56a360451f.description2: Explorers and travellers - starting with T. Falbe and E. Beulé in the early 19th century and continuing through to the end of the 20th century - have been fascinated by interrogating and analysing the remains of one of the most important ancient cities: Carthage. It was conquered by Hassan ibn Nu'man in 698, but was then abandoned by the Arab Muslim population in favour of Tunis, and so for twelve decades was used as a quarry for marble and other stone for the construction of monuments in Tunis and other cities. By the early 20th century only some of what is visible today had been uncovered, namely the baths of Antoninus with their great cisterns, the huge cisterns of La Malga, some sections of the aqueduct connecting Carthage to Zaghwan, the lagoons of the two Punic ports, the remains the amphitheatre and the perimeter of the circus.

9478a32e-0a07-5107-810d-66b32c256277.name: The Post Office
9478a32e-0a07-5107-810d-66b32c256277.history: Designed by the Uruguayan architect Adrien Laforgue, the building has Neo-Moorish aspects and bears many similarities with the Post Office in Algiers, built a few years earlier, and which Laforgue also designed. This was one of the first administrative buildings to be built on Mohammed V Square (formerly Place de Paris).
9478a32e-0a07-5107-810d-66b32c256277.keywords: Moorish style; French in Morocco; French in North Africa; Uruguayan architects in North Africa; protectorate; Islamic art; Islamic architecture; Islamic influence;  Islamic architecture in Morocco; applied arts; ceramic; geometric motifs; arch; column; European architecture; post office; urban planning; technical innovation; postal service; city; urban space; changes in urban spaces; colonial city; colonial building; colonial architecture; colonial economy; city plan; Moroccan city
9478a32e-0a07-5107-810d-66b32c256277.description2: This impressively large administrative building has an entrance formed by two basket arches. These lead to the two entrance doors, both of which are surmounted by an epigraphic band, indicating the services of the institution and highlighted with a rich floral and geometric enamel-green and blue decor. Note that the surroundings of the access doors have recently been painted red-ochre, recalling the colour of houses in Marrakesh. The gallery is supported by columns bearing Ionic capitals. The front is embellished by small semicircular arches in the centre, topped by decorative green *zellige*; the building’s small canopy also has a green-tile frieze.

9533b9d1-3fe7-5fb5-bdef-8dce66c03f06.name: The Black Obelisk of Assyrian King Shalmaneser III
9533b9d1-3fe7-5fb5-bdef-8dce66c03f06.description2: The Black Obelisk of Assyrian King Shalmaneser III was excavated by a British expedition at Nimrud (Iraq) in 1846. There was great excitement when it was found to contain reference to Biblical king Jehu. Furthermore, it depicted his image, still the oldest image of a king of Israel.

954b0597-1e92-5222-bbca-efdc2174af21.name: *The Egyptian Stock Market*
954b0597-1e92-5222-bbca-efdc2174af21.keywords: The Stock Market; Securities Exchange Market; Old Alexandria
954b0597-1e92-5222-bbca-efdc2174af21.description2: An old photograph of the Egyptian Stock Market in Alexandria, one of the oldest stock markets in the world. It was established in 1899, during the time of Khedive `Abbas II, in the Muhammad `Ali square in Alexandria. The Alexandria Stock Market became a landmark in the city that frequently appears on postcards.

9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.name: The Istanbul Main Post Office
9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.notice: This is an unedited Database entry and may contain errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are working to raise the funds required to complete the editing; should you wish to contribute please visit our [Support page](https://www.museumwnf.org/atrium_support.php).
9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.history: The Istanbul Main Post Office is an office building for postal services located at Sirkeci quarter of Fatih district in Istanbul, Turkey. It was designed by architect Vedat Tek in First Turkish National architectural style and was constructed between 1903 and 1909. The four-story building houses a post office, the Sirkeci Post Office, office space for regional administration and also since 2000 the Istanbul Postal Museum. It is Turkey's largest post office building.
9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.keywords: architecture; Vedat Tek; postal service; communication
9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.architects: Architect Vedat Tek; architect Muzaffer Bey
9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.description2: The Istanbul Main Post Office is an office building for postal services located at Sirkeci quarter of Fatih district in Istanbul, Turkey. It was designed by architect Vedat Tek in First Turkish National architectural style and was constructed between 1903 and 1909. The four-story building houses a post office, the Sirkeci Post Office, office space for regional administration and also since 2000 the Istanbul Postal Museum. It is Turkey's largest post office building.

96d75b79-58ff-5945-b11e-11a08e7dd7b9.name: *Typical North African interior*
96d75b79-58ff-5945-b11e-11a08e7dd7b9.archival: Berbrugger, *Algérie Historique Pittoresque et Monumentale*, Paris: J. Delahaye, 1843.

98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.name: Statue of Jules Ferry
98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.holder: Musée d’Histoire Moderne et Contemporaine de Kassar Saïd
98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.keywords: French protectorate of Tunisia; Jules Ferry; Habib Bourguiba
98c08194-bddc-52e4-a6b8-d9483bc9ad1b.description2: This symbolic statue of the French protectorate in Tunisia was located in the centre of the European quarter, between the cathedral and the official residence of the French government, on the Avenue Jules Ferry, today renamed Avenue Habib-Bourguiba. This bronze statue, reaching around three metres in height, is one of the last surviving elements of a monument which had been dedicated to one of the most important thinkers of French imperialism.

9a4c0c9b-0185-5c3b-94c2-863439ee8c9a.name: Istanbul Archaeological Museums
9a4c0c9b-0185-5c3b-94c2-863439ee8c9a.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
9a4c0c9b-0185-5c3b-94c2-863439ee8c9a.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Archaology Museum
9a4c0c9b-0185-5c3b-94c2-863439ee8c9a.description2: In the 19th century, efforts were in place to modernize the Ottoman Empire, as many of the leading statesmen had been exposed to Westernizing ideas through education and travel. This museum was founded by decree as the Imperial Museum (*İmparatorluk Müzesi*) in 1891. The first curator and founder of the museum was Osman Hamdi Bey. Construction of the main building began in 1881, attaining its present neo-Greek form in 1908. The architect was Alexander Vallaury. The site of the museum belonged to the Topkapı Palace outer gardens. It is a prominent structure built in the neoclassical style in Istanbul.

9b43f3ea-5b0a-57f2-be8e-3ff0d20fe6f6.name: Beirut Port during its expansion
9b43f3ea-5b0a-57f2-be8e-3ff0d20fe6f6.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Julien El Khoury
9b43f3ea-5b0a-57f2-be8e-3ff0d20fe6f6.description2: This photograph shows the Beirut port during its expansion, which involved filling areas of sea with rock were brought along the Nahr al-Kalb railway.

9b7af802-1ae8-51cf-9420-82e3e2b1c459.name: Photograph showing Khan Antun Bey Square
9b7af802-1ae8-51cf-9420-82e3e2b1c459.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
9b7af802-1ae8-51cf-9420-82e3e2b1c459.description2: Pictured here is the Khan at Khan Antoun Bey square. The building housed trading offices on the ground and first floors and foreign consulates on the upper floors. There was also an inner courtyard used for parking the consuls' horse-drawn carriages. It was built in 1853 by Antoun Bey Najjar, a merchant who made his fortune in Constantinople. Located by the port, the construction of this building is a reflection of the increasing importance of trade between Beirut and the West following the redevelopment of the port area in 1841. The khan was an important centre for business and trade, and later served many different functions, housing foreign consulates, Ottoman administrative offices, the postal service, merchants' offices and Beirut's first bank.

9d8c93c7-c25d-5dce-a54d-fe8417fb0adc.name: All Saints' Anglican Church
9d8c93c7-c25d-5dce-a54d-fe8417fb0adc.description: All Saints' Church is an English language church founded in the 1870s. Located in the downtown area near the port, today it is overshadowed by high rise construction.
9d8c93c7-c25d-5dce-a54d-fe8417fb0adc.author: Hady El Hajj, Cynthia Karaki, Jennifer Harb
9d8c93c7-c25d-5dce-a54d-fe8417fb0adc.history: This church was first built for marine workers, located by the sea shore near Beirut Port. It later became the church used by the international English-speaking community. The Arab congregation was established later, mainly by Palestinian refugees who were driven from their homes following the 1948 war. Many of these were Lebanese Christians who had been living in Palestine, and joined the Anglican congregation upon their return. All Saints' Church is one of the 27 Anglican/Episcopal churches in the Diocese of Jerusalem and in the Middle East.

9e8a7ea8-8f60-59b4-af77-1fef1a414d6a.name: Construction of the Aswan Dam
9e8a7ea8-8f60-59b4-af77-1fef1a414d6a.description2:
Photograph showing labourers during the construction of the Aswan Dam gates.  
Located in Upper Egypt, the Aswan Dam was the first water storage project in modern times.

9ee00ba7-2731-5d14-b9bf-0d46da259600.name: Ismail, Khedive of Egypt (1830–1895)
9ee00ba7-2731-5d14-b9bf-0d46da259600.keywords: Ismail, Khedive of Egypt; Suez Channel; Great Britain
9ee00ba7-2731-5d14-b9bf-0d46da259600.description2: Portrait of Ismail, Khedive of Egypt (1830–1895), who financed the construction of the Suez Canal. Because of the enormous costs of the building and his reform measures, Egypt's debt rose from three million pounds sterling to 100 million pounds sterling. In 1875 Egypt was bankrupt and Ismail Pasha was forced to sell 176,602 shares to Great Britain for 3,976,582 pounds sterling. Egypt came under financial control of France and Great Britain.

a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.name: 'Zahrat Al-Ihsan School
a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.description: A view of the modern building of Zahrat al-Ihsan school, one of the most renowned Lebanese charitable institutions founded in the nineteenth century to provide education for young girls in Beirut.
a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.author: Hala Masri
a0ae7c32-123a-5f92-8eb4-161510e42915.history: This school was founded by two sisters, Mary Geahchan and Ms Emilie Sursuq. The construction was funded by the donations from the Orthodox Church and first opened on 30 August 1881. Whilst it was originally a school for orphan girls, it later became a private school and became co-educational during the 1975-1990 Lebanese Civil War.

a0d6aa81-6f2f-566c-a687-f570ae278a69.name: Mihrişah Sultan Fountain
a0d6aa81-6f2f-566c-a687-f570ae278a69.description2: Westernisation brought about a change of form and decoration for fountains, which contributed to the urban structure of Istanbul.

a0f99391-e379-547b-847b-d300d897239b.name: Kairouan medina
a0f99391-e379-547b-847b-d300d897239b.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
a0f99391-e379-547b-847b-d300d897239b.history: The Arab Muslims conquerors founded the city of Kairouan in 670 under the orders of Uqba ibn Nafi, as a vital *point d'appui* in their campaign in North Africa. As the first Muslim city in the Maghreb it played a fundamental role in Islamic history, particularly towards the spread of Arab-Islamic civilisation. It remained the region's capital and one of its richest centres of Arab and Islamic culture for five centuries. The value and variety of its archaeological treasures aroused the interest of many European Orientalists in the 19th century. Many did not even hesitate in taking some of the so-called "oriental" aspects of the architecture they saw, and integrating it into their own creations. In fact, the study of Muslim Tunisian heritage saw a significant increase thanks to teh Orientalist architect Henri Saladin in the early 20th century.
a0f99391-e379-547b-847b-d300d897239b.keywords: Orientalism; Oriental architecture; Islamic arts; mosque; mausoleum; world heritage
a0f99391-e379-547b-847b-d300d897239b.description2: Thanks to the value and authenticity of its monuments and the richness and variety of its archaeological treasures, Kairouan can be considered a living museum of Arab and Islamic arts and civilisation. The richness of its monuments' architecture and the variety of its decorations is evidence for the important role Kairouan played in the development of the Islamic arts. Among its most important monuments are the Great Mosque of Uqba ibn Nafi, a masterpiece of universal mosque architecture which was also the foundation of many North African mosques, as well as the Three Doors Mosque with its sculpted façade, the Mausoleum of Sidi Sahbi, and many more. The city was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on the 7 November 1988.

a234f19a-8239-5974-a86e-03dad4940736.name: St Elias Greek Catholic Cathedral
a234f19a-8239-5974-a86e-03dad4940736.description: The Saint Elias Cathedral, which can be found by the al-Najma Square in Downtown Beirut, is affiliated with the Greek Melkite Catholic Church in Lebanon. The cathedral was considered remarkable at the time of its completion in 1863, due to the architect's combination of Byzantine architecture with beautiful other decoration. It is also known for its neo-classical interior, marble iconostasis, Gothic arcs, and the celestial oculi.
a234f19a-8239-5974-a86e-03dad4940736.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
a234f19a-8239-5974-a86e-03dad4940736.history: This cathedral was completed in 1863 and has been visited by a great many pilgrims. It was restored by the Archdiocese in 1994, following a number of damages the structure bore during the Civil War. The works began in late 2003 and were completed in May 2006.
a234f19a-8239-5974-a86e-03dad4940736.keywords: Catholic; Cathedral; Religion; Tourism; Travelling; Saint; Beirut

a318db34-bac0-5d0f-a3b5-606f258a4cf5.name: Ortaköy Mosque
a318db34-bac0-5d0f-a3b5-606f258a4cf5.description2: The original Ortaköy Mosque was built in the 18th century. The current mosque, which was erected in its place, was ordered by the Ottoman Sultan Abdülmecid and built between 1854 and 1856. Its architects were father and son Garabet Amira Balyan and Nigoğayos Balyan (who also designed the nearby Dolmabahçe Palace and the Dolmabahçe Mosque), who designed it in the Neo-Baroque style. It was during the same century that the mosque rose to a higher level of importance on the European side of Istanbul. It is also known as “Great Mecidiye Mosque” and is one of the most beautiful samples of Baroque architecture in Istanbul.

a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.name: Photograph of Bab Idris street
a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.description: Pictured here is Bab Idris street, leading to Bab Idris, the city's western gate and the entrance to the old town. By the time of Ahmad Bey al-Jazzar's reign (1777–1804), the city had four main gates: Bab al-Dirka to the south, Bab al-Santiya to the west, Bab al-Dabbagha to the north, and Bab al-Saraya to the east. Jazzar Pasha built fortifications between these four main gates, which was not a fortified gate. Other city gates included Bab Yaqub, also in the east, Bab Abu Nasr at Burj square, and Bab Idris. These non-military gates are reflections of the city's rapid expansion, particularly due to an increase in trade.
a3c1cda7-3cd5-5acd-9fe6-bbcc3a97be64.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki

a434b4ec-9d28-510b-baac-35beab8f46ee.name: A map of the area around the 'Turkish graveyard' in the town of Livorno (Tuscany). The graveyard is represented as a small green rectangle
a434b4ec-9d28-510b-baac-35beab8f46ee.author: Daniela Tazzi
a434b4ec-9d28-510b-baac-35beab8f46ee.description2: In 1762, Muslims living in Livorno were granted a plot of land outside the city walls, near the beach, to build a graveyard (highlighted in green in the map). The graveyard remained in use until the second half of the 19th century. A Muslim graveyard existed in Livorno even before the 18th century. A significant Muslim community lived in the town. Its first members were captives taken to Italy as slaves. Muslim traders settled in town as well. In 1856, the graveyard was enlarged and surrounded by walls. In 1872 it was demolished to build a road and some of the graves were moved to the city graveyard.

a4ee987f-15bb-56a1-b262-8f402df53ad9.name: *Inside a Jewish household*
a4ee987f-15bb-56a1-b262-8f402df53ad9.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
a4ee987f-15bb-56a1-b262-8f402df53ad9.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
a4ee987f-15bb-56a1-b262-8f402df53ad9.archival: Tunis au XIXe Siècle: Aquarelles et Textes de Charles Lallemand, Apollonia, 2001.
a4ee987f-15bb-56a1-b262-8f402df53ad9.description2: This copy of a beautiful watercolour by Charles Lallemand shows the inside of a bourgeois Jewish household. This snapshot of daily life reveals a great deal of similarity between Jewish and Muslim traditional dress and interiors.

a9007630-d81f-5724-87ad-6fc202c954e3.name: Gufas (Quffas) on the Tigris at Baghdad
a9007630-d81f-5724-87ad-6fc202c954e3.description2: This stereoview by the Keystone company (a reprint from an older negative) was part of a popular box-set of images about Mesopotamia. They were sold across Europe. The text on the reverse contains description of the geography, architecture (explanation of minarets, lament at the absence of fine buildings through devastation of the city by fire, habit of wealthy to live in unpretentious houses to avoid the attention of the Turkish taxman) and history, plus brief caption in half a dozen languages.

a95b3b6a-66a7-5a79-99bd-6be598fec282.name: Dolmabahçe Palace Theatre under construction
a95b3b6a-66a7-5a79-99bd-6be598fec282.author: Bahattin Öztuncay
a95b3b6a-66a7-5a79-99bd-6be598fec282.description2: James Robertson came to Istanbul in 1841 to assist with modernization of the Imperial Mint and remained for 40 years, during which he served without interruption under no less than four Ottoman sultans. He started as head etcher in the Ottoman Mint. Then he began to take photos of Istanbul. He also painted watercolours, and in the early 1850s became interested in photography and went on to become a leading name among early photographers. Robertson’s Istanbul photographs are concerned primarily with the city’s historical monuments. They reveal the city’s magnificent Byzantine and Ottoman structures from different angles and with close-ups taken in an approach that is usually quite aesthetic. In this photo, Dolmabahçe Palace Theatre is seen under construction.

a98c40f6-a4df-55c5-b720-2e843d2d4af6.name: General view of the excavations in the crypt of the Saint-Geneviève monastery, in 1807.
a98c40f6-a4df-55c5-b720-2e843d2d4af6.description2: Although only the library remains today, in the 18th century there used to be a great monasterial complex - the Abbey of Sainte-Geneviève - next to the Church of Saint-Etienne du Mont in Paris. The monastery was destroyed to make space for the construction of the Panthéon and Rue Clovis. The architect Bourla, who was tasked with its demolition, made a great number of sketches and organized many excavations in the crypt, where a number of sarcophagi were discovered. His son Alexandre, who had helped out on the site as a child, worked on the drawings that illustrated the archaeological reports.

abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.name: Café du Marabout in the Souk Ettrouk
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.archival: Copied from a drawing by Sir Grenville Temple, published in his book The Shores and Islands of the Mediterranean in London in 1840, this drawing was taken from Chelli Zouhir, La Tunisie au Rythme des Estampes du Xve au XIXe siecle (Tunis, ed. Tunis Carthage: 1992), p. 65, fig. 25.
abac828d-5728-5fdb-8767-366c5beb8fa5.description2: This copy of a beautiful watercolour from Charles Lallemand's book Tunis et ses Environs shows the Café el-Mourabit in the Turkish souk, also known as the tailors' souk, in the Tunis medina near the Zaytuna Mosque. The café was especially known for its Andalusian architecture. The customers sit on mats sipping coffee, leaning on archways and pillars.

abbd0b79-644c-5895-a661-e0a4ee3109c6.name: Hippodrome, Sultanahmet
abbd0b79-644c-5895-a661-e0a4ee3109c6.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
abbd0b79-644c-5895-a661-e0a4ee3109c6.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul
abbd0b79-644c-5895-a661-e0a4ee3109c6.description2: With the political developments of the 19th century, interest in the East increased steadily in the western world. Everything belonging to the East was the centre of interest for western observers. As a result, close to 160 artists visited Istanbul in the 19th century.

ac19c388-4497-5ec0-878c-c525d8b2c5e0.name: Turbe and Sabil of Mahmud II
ac19c388-4497-5ec0-878c-c525d8b2c5e0.description2: Mahmud II was considered so innovative that his portrait was displayed in public offices and his turbe, built in the Empire style, was in complete sympathy with the ideas of Tanzimat staff.

ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.name: *Khalid ibn al-Walid Mosque*
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum, State Museums
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.author: Stefan Weber
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.second_name: View of the mosque in classical Ottoman revival style from the courtyard
ac262d55-b70d-52be-a08e-76b8060b08ee.description2: This Mosque, built in the early 20th century, was dedicated to Khalid ibn al-Walid, the national hero who conquered Syria for Islam in AD 636. Most of the interior consists out of a single large prayer hall, which contains the domed mausoleum of Khalid ibn al-Walid. It shows over 50 battles he victoriously commanded. The mosque exemplifies the Ottoman architectural style; particularly beautiful are the minarets out of white limestone and the opulent décor inside. Since 2011, the mosque has been a focal point for political opponents protesting against the Syrian government and was damaged.

ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.name: *The Gate of the Roman*
ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.author: Athens 1985, no 205 (F-M Tsigakou)
ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.artist: Théodore Achille Louis, Vicomte du Moncel
ac5b0f5f-98d9-556f-869d-b17cc4a654a2.description2: Since King Otto (1833–1863) made efforts to transform immediately ruinous Athens into a European capital worthy of its erstwhile glory, around the mid-nineteenth century spectacular changes were made in the urban planning structure and morphology of the city. A reliable image of Athens at this time is given by Du Moncel in his book *Vues pittoresques des monuments d’Athenes*. This particular representation of Athens is the Roman Agora (Forum Romanum), natural continuation of the ancient Agora, was built c.10BC, the Gate of Athena Archegetis, which is depicted here. In Ottoman times this Roman gate was known as the Pazaroporta (Bazaar Gate), because it was used as the entrance to the bazaar, the commercial centre of Athens, which occupied the area between the Roman Agora and the Library of Hadrian.

en: Tsigakou, Fani-Maria, *British Images of Greece from the Benaki Museum Collections*, Athens: Benaki Museum, 1995.

acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.name: Musée de Carthage
acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.history: The museum was founded in 1875 on the premises of the Pères Blancs seminary, on the Byrsa Hill near the Saint-Louis Cathedral in Carthage. It was called the Musée Saint-Louis until 1899, and the Musée Lavigerie until 1956. It was given its current name by the Tunisian government following independence and the signing of the Modus Vivendi with the Catholic Church in 1964, at which point they relinquished all rights to the land.
acb1417e-ded5-525f-a850-94113fa99185.description2: The Musée de Carthage houses some of the most beautiful items from the Roman and Punic eras discovered on the Carthage archaeological site since the 19th century. After a long period of restoration, the museum also took on the findings from the UNESCO 1972–75 international arcehological campaign. It offered a new museographic approach, with each of the building's renovated rooms looking onto the beautiful landscape of Tunis Bay. The museum is thematically organised, with rooms dedicated to sculpture, amphoras, mosaics, or rooms reserved especially for works discovered by specific archaeological campaigns on the site.

ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.name: Colonial style building
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.history: In Tunis, the capital of the Protectorate imposed by France on Tunisia in 1881, the European quarter built itself right next to the old Arab medina. A new kind of home - the investment property - soon appeared, and the term balas (from the Italian *palazzo*) became widespread. These two or three-storey housing blocks greatly affected the city's urban landscape by introducing many different architectural styles as well as new architects, designers and builders with from different backgrounds. The 19th century was the century of eclecticism in Tunisia (both neo-classical and neo-baroque), whereas the 20th century was most marked by the influence of Art Nouveau.
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.keywords: Art Nouveau; colonial style; eclecticism; Neo-Baroque
ae85f44d-6a24-58d0-81d8-1e9715c81ac8.description2: 114 Rue de Yougoslavie, the former French Embassy and General Residence previously known as the Disegni building, was designed by the famous architect Auguste Peters, who remains a leading figure of eclecticism. The finely carved balconies, ribbed stone corbels, delicate Venetian style mouldings, overhanging arches and columned galleries all add to the building's majestic character. Auguste Peters was a great master of eclecticism in the first decade of the 20th century, and decorative elements like these characterise his work.

aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.name: The Iwan House
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.description: The house is built around a vestibule, which is flanked on two sides by symmetrical living spaces and open on one end with a tall archway called an *iwan*, or an *'aqd* in the local dialect. It is after this archway that the vestibule is named. The *iwan* archway is usually north facing, for climactic reasons, and built in a broken or curved shape. The vestibule is sometimes T-shaped, with arms at the back leading to two adjacent rooms, or can simply be a wider room, thus becoming more of a central hall.
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.author: Jeff El-Msanne, David Andos
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.history: The architecture of the *iwan* was well suited to both its domestic and economic functions. When opened, it allowed the family to work and sit outside whilst remaining protected from the worst of the winter winds and summer sun. It also facilitated the movement of domestic animals, and the storage of produce and agricultural equipment. The house is built with *ramleh* of stone and limestone-marl from Ashrafiyyeh. Although mud was traditionally used, the walls nowadays are usually covered with reinforced concrete.
aecccc21-db80-57b6-bba8-ea4b65fba9be.keywords: Iwan; Architecture; Arc; Bow; Material; Typology

b0aba8f3-6745-5b4a-b3a4-b7ed8dc1dafe.name: Yıldız Palace Museum
b0aba8f3-6745-5b4a-b3a4-b7ed8dc1dafe.holder: Ministry of Culture and Tourism (General Directorate for Cultural Heritage and Museums)
b0aba8f3-6745-5b4a-b3a4-b7ed8dc1dafe.notice: This is an unedited Database entry and may contain errors and inconsistencies in spelling. We are working to raise the funds required to complete the editing; should you wish to contribute please visit our [Support page](https://www.museumwnf.org/atrium_support.php).
b0aba8f3-6745-5b4a-b3a4-b7ed8dc1dafe.history:
Yildiz Palace, which is the last architectural example of Turkish Ottoman palace, is located on the Yildiz hill in the district of Besiktas. Sultan Ahmed I was the first to build a pavilion, over this land registered at the time to the Private treasury of the Ottoman Sultan as a hunting place sultans beginning during the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566).  
The main construction in the palace started in the period of Sultan Abdulhamid II (1876-1909) and it was called Saray-i Humayun (Central palace). During this period the palace comprised of buildings for private use of the sultan as well as buildings, allocated for the officials, repair shops and carpentry like repairing shop, carpenter’s shop and the buildings of culture and art such as theatre, museum and library. The Palace begun to serve as a museum under the name of “Directorate of the Museum of Yildiz Palace since 1993.
b0aba8f3-6745-5b4a-b3a4-b7ed8dc1dafe.description2: The building, which was opened as a museum on April 8th 1994, consists of a large gallery in 90 meters length. It is understood that the building was used as a museum as indicated by the photos of the reign of Sultan Abdulhamid II (1876-1909) and the valuable objects were exhibited in this residence. Art works, exhibited in the museum belongs to the palace; some of them were taken over while they were in Topkapi Palace. Art works included belongings of Sultan Abdulhamid II, his carpenter tools, gifts given to him and the products of Yildiz Porcelain Factory then.

b0e2a692-ef6a-5333-8e53-cfbbf4c8b01b.name: The first high-rise building in Skopje
b0e2a692-ef6a-5333-8e53-cfbbf4c8b01b.author: Irena Nasteva (niece of Stefan  Nastev)
b0e2a692-ef6a-5333-8e53-cfbbf4c8b01b.history: This was the house of Stefan Nastev, a merchant and owner of the first watermill in Skopje, called Mlin Balkan. During his travels in Vienna, he bought an already worked-out project for construction of a house. His wish was to build a house for his family on the right bank of the Vardar River and he acquired permission from the authorities to do that. The house used to have workshops on the ground floor and an emergency hideout space in the basement, the first one in Skopje. Later the restaurant Pakao was opened in part of the basement. There were wall paintings in the restaurant painted by the renowned painter Nikola Martinoski.
b0e2a692-ef6a-5333-8e53-cfbbf4c8b01b.description2: This house was the first high-rise building constructed in Skopje. Building upon the experience of their predecessors and implementing locally available materials, Macedonian native architects have created their own distinctive style of construction. This structure shows the diversity of the traditional Macedonian urban architecture. It is a five-storey high-rise building of symmetrical type. It has shops on the ground floor. The usable surface of every floor measures 120 square metres. The façade is decorated with garlands and other floral elements, as well as sculptures on the roof.

b0ef4082-e755-5416-9de1-d792e2c9ec9f.name: Tenement
b0ef4082-e755-5416-9de1-d792e2c9ec9f.description: The *wikalat* is a four-storey building with, generally speaking, two apartments per floor. The ground floor is occupied by a shop, and the building is located on a central market street. The central staircase was often built inside a cage. This very rigid separation between the private home and the busy street reflects a new conception between the public and private sphere during this period. If the building included a garden, for example, it was always located at the back of the building. Therefore, the architecture of this building discouraged interaction with the outside world, leaving little access to open air and cutting off the private space from the surrounding environment. This is particularly true of the residences located on the upper floors.
b0ef4082-e755-5416-9de1-d792e2c9ec9f.author: Jeff El-Msanne, David Andos
b0ef4082-e755-5416-9de1-d792e2c9ec9f.history: Two-storey residences emerged in the last decade of the 19th century. Higher, multiple-storey homes were introduced to Beirut after the First World War, following to the arrival of reinforced concrete as an available building material. Although the frame of the building was made of reinforced concrete columns, the walls continued to be built with *ramleh* stone.
b0ef4082-e755-5416-9de1-d792e2c9ec9f.keywords: Tenement; Elevation; Story; House; Architecture; Typology

b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.name: Steam engine building
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.holder: Prussian Palaces (Stiftung Preussische Schlösser und Gärten Berlin Brandenburg)
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.history:
In October 1842 the steam engine in the "Mosque," which could reach 81.4 horsepower, was inaugurated, allowing jets of water from the great fountain in front of Sanssouci Palace to rise to an impressive 38 meters. By possessing what was the most powerful machine in Prussia at the time, built by the young entrepreneur August Borsig, King Frederick William IV hoped to compete with the technical supremacy of England.  
Although today's supply of water to the fountains in Sanssouci Park is provided by means of modern electrical pumps, a visit to the "Mosque" allows the visitor to experience a technical marvel from days past that is still in operation.
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.keywords: Moorish style; Romanticism; Sanssouci; Potsdam; exoticism; steam engine; steam pumping; Frederick William IV; gardens
b1a53072-23dd-58c0-b8c4-495759373b61.description2: The Steam Engine Building, located on a bay of the Havel River called the Neustädter Havelbucht, is at once the most charming as well as the most exotic building in Potsdam. Frederick William IV, the "Romantic on the throne," had it built by Ludwig Persius from 1841-1843, "in the style of the Turkish mosques, with a minaret as a smokestack." The building, which could still be seen at that time from Sanssouci Palace, added a picturesque architectural accent to the Potsdam cultural landscape.

b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.name: Haydarpaşa Train Station
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph Ancient Istanbul; Train Station
b1ada77d-4a0f-5105-a292-423509ecec6b.description2: In 1871 Sultan Abdülaziz ordered a rail line to be built from Haydarpaşa to İzmit. Haydarpaşa station opened in 1872, and in 1888 the Anatolian Railway (CFOA) took over the line and the station. Since the station was built next to the Bosporus, freight trains would unload at Haydarpaşa and the freight would be transferred to ships. Haydarpaşa was chosen to be the northern terminus of the Baghdad Railway and the Hijaz Railway in 1904 and with rail traffic increasing, a new and larger building was required. The Anatolian Railway hired two German architects; Otto Ritter and Helmut Conu to build the new building. They chose a neo-classical structure and construction started in 1906.

b22085c1-312d-582f-860a-c9fff2302d01.name: Tripoli Evangelical School
b22085c1-312d-582f-860a-c9fff2302d01.description: The school consists of an elementary, an intermediate, and a secondary school, each located in separate buildings. The buildings are all examples of typical traditional Lebanese architecture, with white bordered windows and green shutters on the front facades.
b22085c1-312d-582f-860a-c9fff2302d01.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
b22085c1-312d-582f-860a-c9fff2302d01.history: Founded in 1873 by American Protestant Missionaries, Tripoli Evangelical School is one of the oldest high schools in the country, and one of the first pre-higher education institutions in the Middle East. It is located in the city of Tripoli in northern Lebanon, and is part of the National Evangelical Synod of Syria and Lebanon. The school is still in use today, having survived the violent conflicts that have struck Lebanon since its establishment.

b29cbfc5-92ab-5924-883e-7d561e5c7761.name: *Temple and fountain of Zaghwan*
b29cbfc5-92ab-5924-883e-7d561e5c7761.holder: Institut Supérieur d’Histoire Contemporaine de la Tunisie
b29cbfc5-92ab-5924-883e-7d561e5c7761.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar
b29cbfc5-92ab-5924-883e-7d561e5c7761.archival: Copied from a drawinig by Sir Grenville Temple, published in his book The Shores and Islands of the Mediterranean in London in 1840, this drawing was taken from Chelli Zouhir, La Tunisie au Rythme des Estampes du XVe au XIXe siecle (Tunis, ed. Tunis Carthage: 1992), p. 65, fig. 25.
b29cbfc5-92ab-5924-883e-7d561e5c7761.description2: This drawing of the temples and fountains of Zaghwan was drawn by Sir Grenville Temple in the mid-19th century. The triumphal arc and the nymphaeum are carved with two important tales from the city's ancient history. This water temple, located at the feet of Mount Zaghwan, contains a 30 metre long semicircle nymphaeum, bordered on the inside by arched galleries fitted with various niches. At its feet lies a pool, flowing with water which is then carried all the way to Carthage.

b36eb729-4fe6-5e15-afd4-f0f28879427d.name: Fort Rottembourg
b36eb729-4fe6-5e15-afd4-f0f28879427d.history: The Krupp Company provided Sultan Mulay ‘Abd al-‘Aziz (1894-1908) with big guns of the latest model. Fort Rottembourg was named after an officer of the Krupp Company.
b36eb729-4fe6-5e15-afd4-f0f28879427d.keywords: Fortress; German in Morocco; Krupp; steel; industrialisation; industrialists; foreign companies; changes in urban space; modernisation; economy; trade; military architecture
b36eb729-4fe6-5e15-afd4-f0f28879427d.description2: Built on a slight hill on the coast, this fortification is surrounded by deeply sloping masonry ditches. At the foot of the slopes – to enhance the effectiveness of them as defensive barriers – two huge wrought-iron domes cover the command posts from which part of the length of two enormous guns are visible.

b3ffe5a9-b94e-57b4-815b-88dcdb526256.name: *Tomb of Sultan Selim II*
b3ffe5a9-b94e-57b4-815b-88dcdb526256.description2: Although essentially a realist painter, Şevket Dağ worked with free brush stokes in the style of Corot. He is celebrated for his paintings of the interiors of mosques. He took lessons from Osman Hamdi Bey, and followed his master in painting genre pictures reflecting various aspects of Ottoman life. In addition to mosque interiors he would also paint scenes in market places, still-life compositions and the interiors of houses. Over time, Şevket Dağ's work began to be appreciated abroad following exhibitions in European art centres such as Munich and Paris, and he was awarded a gold medal in the Munich International Exhibition of 1909. He later came under the influence of the impressionists.

b4f64de8-89f2-5608-a2d6-f642d0ce7827.name: *Cairo, from the Gate of Citizenib, looking towards the Desert of Suez*
b4f64de8-89f2-5608-a2d6-f642d0ce7827.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
b4f64de8-89f2-5608-a2d6-f642d0ce7827.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
b4f64de8-89f2-5608-a2d6-f642d0ce7827.keywords: Fatimah Khatun; Sultan Khalil; Sayidah Nafisah; Madrasah of Sultan Hassan; Khedive Ismail
b4f64de8-89f2-5608-a2d6-f642d0ce7827.description2: Although entitled 'Cairo from the Gate of Citizenib, looking towards the Desert of Suez', this view actually shows Cairo as seen from Tel Zaynum, situated to the south of the city. The monuments depicted include the tombs of Fatimah Khatun and Sultan Khalil on the left and the mosque of Sayidah Nafisah on the right. In the background, one can discern both the Cairo citadel on the right and the Madrasah of Sultan Hassan on the left. Notwithstanding the incorrect identification of this area of Cairo, the scenes gives a good impression of one of its quarters with its traditional urban architecture and historical monuments before major urban development projects were undertaken under the Khedive Ismail (1863-1879), who was determined to turn Cairo into a modern, international city  on a par with European capitals.
b4f64de8-89f2-5608-a2d6-f642d0ce7827.artist_birthplace: David Roberts: Edinburgh, Scotland; Louis Hague: Tournai, Belgium
b4f64de8-89f2-5608-a2d6-f642d0ce7827.artist_deathplace: David Roberts: London; Louis Hague: London

b5762c66-bf5b-5b77-bfe4-6c9e135ce487.name: *Entrance to a Private Mansion, Cairo*
b5762c66-bf5b-5b77-bfe4-6c9e135ce487.holder: Sharjah Art Museum / Sharjah Museums Department
b5762c66-bf5b-5b77-bfe4-6c9e135ce487.author: Ulrike Al-Khamis
b5762c66-bf5b-5b77-bfe4-6c9e135ce487.description2: The Scottish artist David Roberts spent six weeks in Cairo. In his times, Arab architecture was much less known in Europe than that of ancient pharaonic temples, and Roberts' images of ancient and modern Islamic architecture in Cairo were the first window into this ‘exotic’ world for many Europeans. This image shows the monumental, two tiered, marble entrance portal to a Cairo mansio.Although the entire building is not shown, the composition evokes some of its most characteristic aspects: the walls are high and windowless, protecting the inhabitants' privacy. At the same time, a delicately carved, openwork alcove or mashrabiya projects above the entrance portal to allow air and light into the room behind and to provide those within the chance to observe life outside without being seen themselves. With the arrival of major urban development in Cairo from the mid 13th/ 19th century onwards, many traditional buildings were either erased or modified to reflect the new European-style tastes of the urban elite. In the process, the traditional courtyard-style layout of Cairene houses was was often replaced by European-style designs, and traditional architectural elements like mashrabiyas made way for the latest in European technology, including glass pane windows.
